10031-the-complete-poetical-works-of-edg:
John H. Ingram edited this collection of Edgar Allan Poe's complete poetical works, aiming to improve on the verbatim reprints of the first posthumous collection of 1850. In 1874 Ingram had drawn attention to unknown and unreprinted Poe poems, and many of them appear here.

The volume groups poems of later life, manhood, and youth, with scenes from Politian, doubtful poems, prose poems, and a memoir of Poe. Readers find The Raven's companions in full: musical, gloomy, and strange. It remains a useful edition for anyone who wants Poe's poetry whole, with an editor who knew the manuscripts.
10330-fruitfulness:
Emile Zola published Fruitfulness in French as Fecundite, translated here by Ernest Alfred Vizetelly in 1900. It opens a planned four-book poem on the principles of human life: fruitfulness, work, truth, and justice. The hero is Matthew, first of four brothers named for the evangelists.

Zola argues that the home creates the city, the city the fatherland, and science-led love of country a wider human fatherland. Family, labor, and thought thus form one moral chain. Readers get a vast, idealistic novel of fertility, home, and social hope, in Zola's bold naturalist style.
10381-the-history-of-a-crime-the-testimo:
Victor Hugo wrote this eyewitness history of Louis Bonaparte's coup of December 2, 1851, translated by T. H. Joyce and Arthur Locker. Hugo, then in exile, tells how the republic was seized in a night of arrests, placards, and street fighting. His voice is that of a witness and a judge at once.

Day by day, Hugo follows the ambush, the struggle at barricades, and the massacre that followed. Representatives are hunted, Baudin falls, and Paris learns the price of resistance. Readers get a fierce, detailed indictment of a coup, and a classic of political witness.
10510-inaugural-presidential-address:
William Jefferson Clinton gave this inaugural address at noon on January 20, 1993, in about fifteen minutes and sixteen hundred words. Clinton, a new president after the Cold War, speaks of American renewal in the depth of winter, forcing spring by words and faces shown to the world. The speech is short, hopeful, and plain.

Clinton salutes his predecessor, George Bush, for half a century of service, and thanks those who beat depression, fascism, and communism. He warns that freedom's sunshine still faces ancient hatreds and new plagues, and that change must preserve ideals. Readers get a landmark speech of a new generation taking power.
10881-crescent-and-iron-cross:
E. F. Benson wrote this wartime account of Turkey and its German alliance during the First World War. Drawing on official papers, the testimony collected by Lord Bryce, and other published sources, he traces Ottoman rule, the Armenian massacres, and Germany's growing sway at Constantinople. Material gathering stopped in June 1917, so the book speaks from inside the war, not after it.

Chapters move from history to current events, covering famine and disease in Arab lands, the policing of the Syrian coast, and Allied pledges to end Turkish rule over subject peoples. Benson also guesses how that pledge might be carried out. The result is both a wartime argument and a record of what British readers were told about Turkey before the fighting ended.
10932-over-the-pass:
Frederick Palmer's 1912 novel follows Jack Wingfield from the Arizona desert to New York wealth and back again. A young man raised around the Galeria Pass, Jack rides, carries mail, and drifts among prospectors before family money and a father's expectations pull him east. The story is split into three parts: easy travelling, finding himself, and finding his place in life.

Mary, Prather, and the Wingfield family press Jack toward duty, marriage, and business, while the open country keeps calling him back. Palmer writes the desert with care, from dry air and mountain passes to camp life and mining towns. The novel asks what a restless young man owes his family, and whether fortune can replace the freedom he left behind.
11259-polly-and-the-princess:
Emma C. Dowd's 1917 novel follows Polly Dudley, a cheerful young woman who arrives at the June Holiday Home, a retreat where indigent gentlewomen wait for the last train. Polly's energy disrupts the home's waffle mornings and strict routines, and chapters follow her addresses to the board. a hiking club, a moonshine party, and a mystery involving a princess and a dragon. Doodles, a singing companion, adds comedy.

Dowd wrote Polly as the center of a series, and this book leans on her warmth and tact. The plot is light, but its setting matters: a home for women with little money, run by rules and gossip. Readers who enjoy early twentieth-century girls' fiction will find Polly's good humor the main attraction.
11279-the-slim-princess:
George Ade's 1907 comic novel, expanded from a Saturday Evening Post story of 1906, is set in the imaginary Balkan state of Morovenia, where mosques and motor-cars share the landscape. Princess Kalora suffers an affliction in Morovenian eyes: she is slim, while local law and custom prize plumpness. Her story moves from garden parties and messengers to Washington, D.C., and a homecoming by cable.

Ade uses the invented kingdom to satirize both Oriental custom and American modernity, with champagne-drinking title holders and fez-wearing traditionalists side by side. The humor is broad and affectionate rather than bitter. The novel shows Ade's gift for turning a social absurdity into a sustained joke.
11451-the-rome-express:
Arthur Griffiths's 1907 mystery The Rome Express opens as the direttissimo approaches Paris one March morning, with something very much amiss in the sleeping car. Between Laroche and Paris, a hundred miles without stop, seven occupants had breakfasted, six seen in the restaurant, the seventh a lady unmoved. On return, passengers dress for arrival, calls for the porter go unanswered, and the attendant is found asleep, snoring in his bunk. Two passengers, the lady in berths nine and ten and another man, still make no sign.

Griffiths, a former prison official turned novelist, builds a classic train mystery from a closed car and a missing porter. Twenty chapters follow the investigation. Readers of Edwardian detective fiction will enjoy its railway setting and careful, procedural pace.
11504-further-foolishness:
Stephen Leacock's 1916 Further Foolishness, sketches and satires on the follies of the day, divides into fiction follies, movies and motors, peace, war, and politics, and timid thoughts on timely topics. Contents include stories shorter still, the Snoopopaths or fifty stories in one, Serge the Superman translated with a hand pump from Russian. Madeline of the Movies done back into words, the call of the carburettor, a grass bachelor's guide, Germany from within out, merry Mexico, and are the rich happy.

Leacock opens by meeting the demand for shorter stories at its source, promising tales that swell to dollar-fifty novels if soaked overnight in rainwater. His parodies are gentle and precise. Readers of Canadian humor will find Leacock mocking modern life without bitterness.
11549-the-life-and-letters-of-elizabeth-:
George L. Prentiss wrote this memoir of his wife Elizabeth Prentiss, author of Stepping Heavenward, at the request of her trusted friends. Her letters, with extracts from her journals, form the larger part of the book, running from her twentieth year almost to her last hour.

A plain narrative links the letters, with memories of her home, her friends, and the books she wrote, plus a sketch of her father. The result is a picture of a Christian home life in its changing scenes, offered, as the preface hopes, to readers who welcomed Stepping Heavenward into their own homes.
11746-through-the-brazilian-wilderness:
Theodore Roosevelt's Through the Brazilian Wilderness opens in 1908, as his presidential term closed, when Father Zahm called on him. Zahm, an Ohio boy schooled in a log schoolhouse, loved Dante, history, and science, and Roosevelt praised his book on evolution and dogma.

Later pages follow the expedition into Brazil, with houses holding several families, children loved by all, and good manners without privacy. Boys do not bully girls or smaller boys, and girls early wear the loin-cloth. The book is Roosevelt's account of a river journey, natural history, and the people met along the way, written after the presidency.
12-through-the-looking-glass:
Alice steps through a mirror into a land laid out like a chessboard. Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass, sequel to Wonderland, moves its heroine square by square toward queenship. A prefatory game maps her eleven moves across the board.

She meets Tweedledum and Tweedledee, Humpty Dumpty, and the White Knight on the way. Jabberwocky, the Walrus and the Carpenter, and the looking-glass insects fill the squares. The book closes with a feast, a coronation, and a question: was it all a dream, and whose? Word games, reversed logic, and chess rules blend into a dream that rewards rereading at any age.
1220-the-atheist-s-mass:
Honoré de Balzac tells of Desplein, a great Paris surgeon and a proud atheist, who is seen paying for masses to be said for a dead man. A young student begs to know why, and Desplein tells of a poor water-carrier whose faith and kindness once saved him, and of the debt he still pays.

The short tale turns on a paradox: the atheist keeps faith with a friend through the Church he scorns. Balzac writes Paris medicine and charity with his usual detail. The story is brief and moving, and it shows Balzac at his most humane.
12741-risen-from-the-ranks-or-harry-walt:
Horatio Alger's 1874 novel continues Harry Walton's story from Bound to Rise, following a poor boy's climb by steady work. Harry, now a young man, speaks, studies, and earns his way, avoiding the freak luck Alger says real boys cannot count on. A debating society scene, where he recites a poem on Shamus O'Brien, shows his pluck.

Alger dedicates the tale to boys like Harry, hoping to prove that will and work open a path from the ranks. The story, partly suggested by a famous editor's career, moves through offices, lodgings, and small triumphs. It is classic Alger: plain, earnest, and meant to encourage.
13034-mary-minds-her-business:
George Weston's Mary Minds Her Business, published in 1920, opens with a preface on heroine Mary Spencer's forebears. In the late seventeenth century a blacksmith named Josiah Spencer, quick of eye, hand, and temper, married Mary McMillan. He bought five hundred acres on each side of the Quinebaug ford from chief Oeneko, and built a shop on the Hartford to Providence road. Business followed.

The modern Mary faces an annual report showing an alarming loss, with Judge Cutler frowning over too many improvements and office glances averted in shame. Weston blends family saga with business story. The novel follows a woman taking charge of Spencer and Son.
1322-leaves-of-grass:
Walt Whitman was the American poet who sang himself and his country. He gathers his life's work in Leaves of Grass. "Song of Myself," "Crossing Brooklyn Ferry," and "Out of the Cradle" stand beside the Civil War elegies, in free verse that broke every rule of its age.

Whitman writes of the body, the soul, democracy, and death with a prophet's breadth and a worker's plain speech. The book grew through edition after edition, and it remade American poetry. It stands as the great American poem, and it still reads as fresh and bold.
13288-a-great-success:
Mrs. Humphry Ward's 1916 Great Success, from Hearst's International Library, follows Arthur and Doris Meadows, a young couple in a small South Kensington house. It opens with Doris in consternation: Arthur tipped a taxi driver half a crown on a fare of one and twopence. Doris then ran to the window crying hi to get it back. Ward writes society comedy with a keen eye.

Later, Doris watches Meadows and Lady Dunstable cross the lawn. She advises herself to hold her own, play no games she dislikes, and go to church if she wishes, since Lady Dunstable is a heathen. A recitation scene breaks into a loud, uncontrollable laugh from young Dunstable, while Madame Vavasour throws off her stage trance in a thunderous frown. The novel is a witty portrait of marriage and society.
14084-a-vindication-of-the-press:
Daniel Defoe's 1718 Vindication of the Press appears here in the Augustan Reprint Society edition of 1951, introduced by Otho Clinton Williams. Defoe defends writers against critics who live by attacking them, arguing that scandal can be a backhanded honor. Dryden, persecuted by envy for years, and Pope, lesser but still fine, show how abuse keeps authors alive in public talk.

Craft advice runs beside polemic. Hasty writers ruin themselves with blunders, though a kind printer may take the errata on himself. Prose tolerates a quick look, but poetry demands repeated care, since harmony, simile, and strong sense take time to join. Critics, Defoe jokes, permit no one to blunder but themselves. Short and sharp, the pamphlet still speaks to writers: work slowly, expect envy, and let the work answer its foes.
14589-certain-success:
Norval A. Hawkins, author of The Selling Process, published Certain Success in Detroit in 1920, in a third edition, as a manual for salesmen who wanted to sell themselves as well as goods. The chapters run from studying to celebration.

Hawkins teaches how to study prospects, gain a chance, read other men, and knock at the door of opportunity, with advice on eyes, voice, and manner in the interview. He treats the salesman himself as the product. The book is brisk early twentieth-century business counsel, confident and practical, with the optimism of its era.
15000-the-life-of-reason-the-phases-of-h:
George Santayana's Life of Reason, in five volumes, gathers Reason in Common Sense and four companion volumes under one title: the phases of human progress. Its opening defines progress as relative to an ideal reflection creates, and reason as efficacious reflection justified by its fruits in consciousness.

The life of reason names all practical thought and action, the sum of art, with a natural basis that makes it definable. Modern philosophy, Santayana argues, is not helpful, positivism offers no positive ideal, Christian philosophy is mythical in misrepresenting facts, and liberal theology takes a superstitious attitude toward a natural world. The work remains a major American philosophy text.
15055-the-free-rangers-a-story-of-the-ea:
Joseph A. Altsheler's 1909 frontier novel follows two boys and their comrades along the Mississippi in early American days. Though it stands alone, it carries on from his Young Trailers, Forest Runners, and related books. The action runs from forest trails to a Spanish chateau and on to New Orleans.

Canoe chases, a captured galleon, battles, storms, and a white stallion keep the pace high, while Paul's talks with a Spaniard add a note of diplomacy. Altsheler writes for young readers who love the woods and the river. The novel blends history, danger, and friendship in the classic frontier style.
1562-little-rivers-a-book-of-essays-in-p:
Henry Van Dyke's essays in profitable idleness celebrate rivers, fishing, and the art of doing nothing well. A prelude and a dedication to his little daughter Brooke open the book. Chapters follow the Ristigouche by horse-yacht, trout fishing in the Traun, and quiet walks by heather and balsam boughs.

Van Dyke writes of angling as a school of patience, and of nature as a cure for hurry, with a minister's warmth and a poet's eye. The essays are gentle and unhurried. They offer a classic of American outdoor writing, best read slowly, like the rivers they praise.
15629-the-southern-cross:
Foxhall Daingerfield Jr. wrote this play in four acts, The Southern Cross, produced at the Opera House in Lexington, Kentucky, on April 13, 1909, for the benefit of the Morgan Monument. J. L. Richardson and Company of Lexington printed it, copyrighted in 1909, and Daingerfield dedicated it to the memory of General John Hunt Morgan. The play belongs to the Bryan Station Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution.

The people of the play include Gordon Cabell, Carter Hilliary, Colonel Philip Stuart and his son George, Beverly Stuart called Bev, and Stephen Winthrop of the 12th Massachusetts. Fairfax Stuart called Fair, Mrs. Stuart, Charlotte Hilliary, and Aunt Marthy complete the cast, with soldiers of the 12th Massachusetts and a prison guard. The play stages a Civil War story of Kentucky, prison, and loyalty, written for a local audience honoring Morgan's raiders.
16377-the-blue-book-of-chess:
This 1910 handbook teaches chess from the ground up: the board, the moves and powers of each piece, notation, the laws of the game, and maxims for beginners. Openings follow in detail, from the King's Knight's Opening and Evans Gambit to the Ruy Lopez and the Two Knights' Defence. Eighty-five illustrative games, played by Morphy, Anderssen, and others, show the lines in action.

The book is practical and thorough, made for a player who wants to learn openings properly rather than by guesswork. Diagrams and game scores fill the pages. For club players and students of classic chess, it remains a solid old manual from the age of Morphy.
16502-the-witness:
Grace Livingston Hill Lutz opens this 1917 novel in a boys' dormitory thrown into uproar, where Paul Courtland steps out to see the fun. The tale that follows is a Christian romance of school and home life, built on the text from First John: he that believes has the witness in himself. Faith, friendship, and young love drive the plot.

Hill Lutz writes in her warm, earnest style, with clear morals and lively scenes of schoolboy life. The book was a popular hit of its day, aimed at families and young readers. Those who enjoy old-fashioned inspirational fiction will find it gentle, sincere, and easy to read.
16567-aunt-jane-s-nieces-in-the-red-cros:
Edith Van Dyne sends the nieces into Red Cross war work in this 1915 volume. Patricia Doyle asks Uncle for the news at breakfast in Willing Square. The tale runs from the arrival of a boy and a girl through Doctor Gys's decision, a hospital ship, and the firing line. Little Maurie, the coward, war's victims, and a capture follow.

Van Dyne writes brisk, warm adventure for girls, with nursing, courage, and loyalty at the center. The book belongs to the war years, when series heroines took up service. Readers of the series will find the same plucky spirit, now on a hospital ship near the fray.
16778-pulpit-and-press:
Mary Baker Eddy wrote this 1895 book on Christian Science, issued by the trustees under her will in Boston. It holds a dedication sermon, notes on her textbook, hymns such as Feed My Sheep, and a long set of press clips from Chicago, Boston, and other papers. The book is dedicated to two thousand six hundred children whose gifts paid for the Mother's Room in her Boston church.

Eddy pairs pulpit words with press praise, letting papers speak for the faith as well as her own voice. The clips show how the new church was seen by outsiders in its early years. The book works as both church record and scrapbook, and it gives a clear view of Christian Science at a moment of growth.
1688-the-people-of-the-abyss:
Jack London went down into the East End of London in 1902 dressed as a workman, slept in doss-houses, and queued at the casual ward known as the spike. He stood in line for bread and skilly. He wrote what he saw at street level: men out of work, women carrying the household on pennies, and children growing up hungry in rooms that never dried out.

The chapters move from lodging houses to hop-picking in Kent and back to the London streets. London argues throughout that the poor are not idle but trapped by wages too low to live on. It remains a first-hand record of Edwardian poverty, blunt, angry, and grounded in nights the author himself spent among the people he describes.
17011-i-n-r-i-a-prisoner-s-story-of-the-:
Peter Rosegger's novel, translated by Elizabeth Lee, opens in a crowded square before a law court, where a crowd waits for a verdict on a prisoner. Talk swings between doom and freedom as people wager on what the man did and what he meant to do. The prologue sets up a tale of crime, faith, and the cross that gives the book its name.

Rosegger, an Austrian writer of peasant life, builds the story around guilt, judgment, and grace rather than mere court drama. The prose is earnest and moving, with crowd scenes that feel true. Readers who like moral tales with a strong heart will find a thoughtful, old-style novel about sin and mercy.
17545-princess:
M. G. McClelland, author of Oblivion and Jean Monteith, published this novel in New York in 1886 with the United States Book Company, as number seventeen of the American Authors' Series. McClelland dedicates the book with love and admiration to the memory of Thomas Alexander Seddon. The story opens when the idea of a removal to Virginia is first raised in the family of General Percival Smith.

Smith, an ex-brigadier in the United States service, faces consternation at the move, and the novel follows the family's Virginia life. Readers get a post-war American society novel, with a heroine at its centre. The book suits readers of forgotten American fiction of the 1880s.
18018-the-free-press:
Hilaire Belloc wrote The Free Press in 1918, first run in The New Age, and dedicated to its editor, A. R. Orage. Belloc argues that a free press means papers free from the grip of big business, ads, and party machines, not merely papers free from the censor.

He praises The New Age and Chesterton's New Witness as the two London papers where hard truths about corrupt politics could still be told. Both were small, poor, and little read, yet their words moved events. Belloc's essay is sharp, partisan, and still quoted, a classic case for a press that serves readers, not owners.
18116-the-freebooters-of-the-wilderness:
Agnes C. Laut wrote The Freebooters of the Wilderness in 1913, published in New York by Moffat, Yard. Laut, author of The Conquest of the Great Northwest, sets this novel on the Canadian frontier, where law is slow and freebooters move fast.

Chapters run from a choice to straddle or fight, through stacked cards, a victim of law's delay, and eight into might, to the long trail and the game trail. Men play unconscious parts while crime scores and the majesty of law veils itself. Laut writes with a historian's eye and a novelist's pace. It is a bold, western tale of justice on the edge.
1813-a-man-of-business:
Paris had a polite word, lorette, for a kept woman. This tale follows the money that flows around one: debts bought up, lawyers hired, and a life priced piece by piece. Desroches the lawyer, Cerizet the bailiff's man, and Maxime, whose debts have been bought up by a firm, move through a Paris where a debt is a weapon.

The tale, dedicated to Baron James de Rothschild, is a study of the business of ruin: how creditors, lawyers, and lovers trade claims on a man's future. Balzac writes the financial machinery with the same care he gives to drawing rooms. The novella's bite comes from its calm tone — a whole life priced, parcelled, and sold.
20210-shakespeare-s-christmas-gift-to-qu:
Anna Benneson McMahan wrote Shakespeare's Christmas Gift to Queen Bess, set in 1596. London's Mermaid Tavern glitters with diamond panes in chill December air. The Mermaid Club holds its last meeting of that year there. Not a member is absent, and expectation stands on tiptoe.

The club drew wits, poets, and players of Shakespeare's London circle. A Christmas gift for Queen Elizabeth forms the tale's bright core. McMahan blends known history with warm, invented tavern scenes. Readers get a festive glimpse of the Bard's world at holiday time. The tale first appeared in print long after Shakespeare's own age had passed.
20243-dross:
Henry Seton Merriman wrote Dross, a novel set amid the fall of old France. One scene marks a hundred years since Napoleon the First was born. A gathering of mushroom nobility, soldiers, and diplomats marks that day. Merriman calls Napoleon the greatest mushroom sprung from hotbed strife.

New men rose fast in that age, and fell just as fast. Dross, the worthless stuff skimmed from metal, names what time leaves behind. Merriman's tales turn on honor, politics, and men tested by change. Readers get taut historical fiction from a skilled, spare storyteller.
20533-jill-the-reckless:
Jill the Reckless is a comic novel by P. G. Wodehouse, filled with his young men about town and their cheerful disasters. It opens the morning after a party. Freddie asks that the coffee stay where it is: café noir for him this morning, as noir as it can jolly well stick.

As far as he can remember, it was Ronny Devereux's birthday, or something. From such hazy starts, Jill's story runs through lost fortunes, stage work, and romance on both sides of the Atlantic. Wodehouse keeps the tone feather-light while his heroine proves anything but reckless where it counts.
20608-how-to-get-on-in-the-world-a-ladde:
Major A. R. Calhoun's How to Get On in the World, published in 1895, calls itself a ladder to practical success. It belongs to the great shelf of Victorian self-help. Young men starting in trade were its first readers, and it speaks to them as a friendly drillmaster.

To win, Calhoun writes, we must begin the struggle with a high purpose. Only then are we and the world the better for our having lived. We should keep before our minds the characters and methods of the noble men who succeeded along the same lines. The ladder is climbed, he insists, by character more than by luck.
20698-the-story-of-glass:
Sara Ware Bassett's The Story of Glass teaches a great industry through a story for young readers. Glassmaking becomes clear as the heroine, Jean, follows it from sand to finished ware. Bassett wrote a row of such books, each built around American work.

Jean is sent to Boston for school, since the story holds it right for an American girl to go to school. She is put in charge of her uncle, Mr. Uncle Bob, as the family calls him. Uncle Bob is delighted with the arrangement, for they are great friends. Through Jean's visits and questions, the furnaces and blowers of the glassworks come alive.
20993-sir-ludar-a-story-of-the-days-of-t:
A parsonage nursery of nine-year-olds bows to a brother king in Sir Ludar. Talbot Baines Reed sets his tale in the days of great Queen Bess. The young teller owns he has clean forgotten his own birth's tale.

Elizabethan England, with its courts, roads, and sea dogs, stages the adventure. Ludar's path runs through peril, loyalty, and Tudor pomp in Reed's brisk hand. Reed loved to dress schoolboy virtues in period garb for his readers. Sir Ludar shows that blend at its best, history taught as a rattling tale of the Virgin Queen's reign.
21111-wild-nature-won-by-kindness:
Mrs Brightwen, vice-president of the Selborne Society, gathered these short nature papers into a book. It was first issued in the 1890s and reprinted in an eighth edition in 1898. She dedicated it to surgeon Sir James Paget, whose encouragement she credits for the writing. Her subject is the wildlife of her house and garden.

Close, patient watching is her method: kindness, she argues, wins the trust of wild creatures better than traps or cages. Later editions added chapters on an ant-lion and a tame toad. The papers model the Selborne idea of studying nature where you live, with notebooks, patience, and care for each small life.
21189-aesop-in-rhyme-old-friends-in-a-ne:
Marmaduke Park put Aesop's fables into verse in this Philadelphia children's book of 1852, calling them old friends in a new dress. The Dog and the Wolf opens the set: a lean, hungry wolf envies a plump, well-fed dog until he hears about the chain. Each fable becomes a short rhymed tale.

Park aimed the rhymes at young readers who might find prose morals dry. The fables keep their old plots and pointed endings, now carried by metre and rhyme. Illustrations from the University of Florida copy support the text. It is a neat sample of how American publishers repackaged classic tales for children.
21219-a-voice-in-the-wilderness:
Grace Livingston Hill's 1916 novel opens at night, when Margaret Earle climbs down from a stopped train into rough darkness with no platform in sight. She is a young eastern schoolteacher come to the wild West, and the train seems to have left her in the middle of nowhere. Her heavy suitcase is her only company.

Hill, author of Marcia Schuyler, built Christian romances around brave young women in hard settings. Margaret must find her school, her pupils, and her footing in a rough land, helped by the people of the place. Faith and love grow together as the wilderness voice of the title calls her.
21259-the-black-cross:
Olive M. Briggs opens her 1909 novel on a winter night in St. Petersburg, with snow crowning the domes and sleigh bells filling the Morskaia. Crowds surge toward the Mariinsky Theatre, but for the first time in memory no ballet will be given. Instead a violinist named Velasco is to play.

No musician in all the Russias, the story says, could play like Velasco, and his instrument seems to have the gift of tears. The frontispiece cry, Ah, mein Gott, it is Kaya, hints at the personal drama behind the music. Briggs builds a romantic tale of art, fame, and buried identity in imperial Russia.
21263-on-the-old-road-vol-2-of-2-a-colle:
John Ruskin's miscellaneous essays and articles on art and literature, written between 1834 and 1885, fill this second volume of On the Old Road. Parliamentary evidence opens it: Ruskin testifying on the National Gallery site in 1857, public institutions in 1860, and the Royal Academy Commission. A piece on what a museum or picture gallery should be follows.

Minor art writings treat the Cavalli monuments and Verona and its rivers, with a catalogue. Then the subject jumps: the colour of the Rhine, the strata of Mont Blanc, the temperature of spring water, and the stratified Alps of Savoy. The range shows Ruskin's two lifelong studies, art and mountains.
2132-the-daughter-of-an-empress:
Louise Muhlbach, writing historical romance, follows a daughter of an empress through the Russian court, where counts, favourites, and conspiracies crowd around the throne. Chapters move from Countess Natalie Dolgorucki to Princess Elizabeth and the regent Anna. Muhlbach wrote many historical romances, using real courts as stages for invented heroines.

Court balls, pencil sketches, revolutions, and dooming letters carry the plot through weddings, punishments, and diplomatic quarrels. Muhlbach blends real figures with invented scenes, and the novel reads as a colourful pageant of eighteenth-century Russia. The Russian court, with its guards, favourites, and sudden falls, suits her taste for drama.
21689-the-tyranny-of-weakness:
Charles Neville Buck sets The Tyranny of Weakness in the Valley of Virginia, in a tale copyrighted in 1917. Stuart's knightly heritage must not be made a joke, the hero holds. The girl who teases him finds his blazing eyes more diverting than his calm moods.

Buck, who wrote The Call of the Cumberlands, opens with two types in embryo. A grain of wheat and a poppy seed, side by side, stand for their fates. Paul Stahr draws the frontispiece for Watt of New York. Love, pride, and the weakness that rules strong men drive this mountain romance.
21715-away-in-the-wilderness:
Hunter Jasper Derry looks out over wild country in the opening of this short Ballantyne tale of the North American backwoods. Jasper is known as the best hunter and boldest trapper among his friends, yet he is gentle and quiet by nature. His leather coat, moccasins, knife, and hatchet mark him as a man who lives off the land.

Ballantyne drew on his own years in Canada for scenes like these. The story follows Jasper through the woods he knows so well, where skill and calm matter more than noise. It is a compact tale of backwoods life, written for readers who loved his longer fur-trade books.
21797-a-sailor-s-lass:
A fisherman's family lives in a boat turned into a cottage in this tale by Emma Leslie, a writer of stories for the young. Wooden walls and a roof of planks and tarpaulin make the old hull a home. Four chains hold it to posts in the ground, yet in the great gales it floats and strains like a ship. One stormy night the wife lies awake while her husband snores on.

Their daughter, the sailor's lass of the title, stands at the center of the family's hopes. Chapters move through bad times, a tea meeting, and brighter days. Leslie wrote for Sunday readers, and faith runs through the hardship. It is a tender picture of poor fishing folk on the English coast.
219-heart-of-darkness:
Marlow, waiting on the Thames yawl Nellie, tells of a river journey into the Congo. Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness follows Marlow upriver to find Kurtz, an ivory agent gone beyond law and mercy. Stations, fog, and drumbeats mark the passage inward.

Kurtz's genius and horror force Marlow to face what empire does to men. Conrad's dense, shifting prose leaves judgments open and uneasy. The novella's view of Africa has drawn strong criticism for its silences. It remains a central, troubling work of modern fiction. Conrad's river tale has inspired films, essays, and fierce debate for over a century.
21992-christianity-and-progress:
Christianity must learn to live with progress, argues Harry Emerson Fosdick in his Cole Lectures at Vanderbilt University, published in 1922. Fosdick, professor at Union Theological Seminary and preacher at First Presbyterian in New York, became the best-known liberal voice in American pulpits. He opens with a fish that never notices water and a bird that never notices air. We are all, he says, capable of that same unawareness inside our own element.

The lectures defend a Christianity that can grow with knowledge rather than fear it. The Cole foundation required lectures in defense and advocacy of the Christian religion. Fosdick's answer helped define liberal Protestantism for a generation. His tone is calm, clear, and certain that faith and modern thought can be reconciled.
22170-five-lectures-on-blindness:
Kate M. Foley, home teacher for the California State Library, delivered these Five Lectures on Blindness in 1919. Foley was herself blind. She had studied at the California School for the Blind. She taught as a volunteer. Then she carried books and lessons to blind people in their homes. The state library printed her lectures at Sacramento.

She tells sighted readers what blindness is, and what it is not. Training, Braille, work, and cheerfulness stand at the centre of her counsel. Foley scolds pity and praises independence from long personal experience. Her lectures remain a clear early statement by a blind professional on the education of her own community.
22189-parables-of-the-cross:
I. Lilias Trotter, an artist who became a missionary in Algeria, wrote Parables of the Cross as a devotional meditation. Trotter found her lesson in a plant's growth. Budding, blossoming, and seed-bearing taught her the power of death that sets life free. She insists the image is no far-fetched fancy, but one of God's many voices in nature.

Short chapters follow the plant through its dying and fruiting. Each stage becomes a parable of self given up and life multiplied. Trotter's prose is quiet, intense, and full of the desert light she lived in. The little book has been reprinted by mission societies ever since, a classic of its contemplative kind.
2233-a-damsel-in-distress:
P. G. Wodehouse turns a country house romance into pure farce when a young woman in trouble meets a cheerful American songwriter. A Damsel in Distress moves between London streets and a grand English estate, where aunts, butlers, and secret passages conspire against true love. Wodehouse keeps the plot spinning with mistaken identity and timely rescues.

The humor lies in the gap between high drama and low comedy: heroines declare, heroes bumble, and servants quietly save the day. Light, witty, and perfectly paced, the novel shows Wodehouse at his sunny best. It is an ideal read for anyone who wants romance with laughter rather than tears.
23010-gulmore-the-boss:
College learning draws laughter in Gulmore, the Boss, a tale by Frank Harris. Oh yes, he's smart, a young woman says of the professor. Greek, Latin, German, and much more besides fill the professor's head, the speaker says. Older students claimed he outknew his colleagues combined. He shares that opinion, she adds, laughing, then blushing at her own laugh.

Gulmore's authority, over students and perhaps over the speaker, shapes the story's tension. Harris liked strong men and the women who sized them up, and his campus boss fits the pattern. The blush in the excerpt matters, embarrassment covering admiration. Behind the talk stands a study of power in a small academic world, told with Harris's usual confidence.
2325-the-iceberg-express:
David Cory's Iceberg Express is a children's adventure in which a boy's imagination turns an iceberg into a train bound for the frozen north. The story races through Arctic wonders with the cheerful nonsense of early children's fantasy, where geography bends to fun. Cory, creator of the Puss in Boots Jr. books, keeps the tone light.

Young readers of its era enjoyed the mix of travel, animals, and mild peril. The book now reads as a period curiosity with charm. It suits collectors of early children's books and nostalgic readers alike.
23296-the-fighting-shepherdess:
Caroline Lockhart wrote this western novel of a fighting shepherdess, published in New York with a frontispiece by M. Leone Bracker. Kate, the heroine, sits on a rock as a dark silhouette against the sky, a sheepwoman holding her own in a man's range war.

Lockhart, who also wrote The Lady Doc, knew western ranch life firsthand, and her heroine fights with grit, humor, and skill. The novel stands out for a woman hero who works, rides, and wins on the open range. Lockhart knew ranch life firsthand, so her heroine's grit rings true. Kate wins Mrs Toomey's true-blue answer and lifts the woman to her feet in gratitude.
2361-why-go-to-college-an-address:
Alice Freeman Palmer, former president of Wellesley College, answers the question of her title with warmth and conviction. Why Go to College? argues that higher education enlarges a life, especially for young women newly admitted to its doors, by training judgment, widening friendship, and opening useful work. Palmer speaks from experience, not theory.

Her address is short, direct, and still persuasive more than a century on. She treats college as a public good as well as a private one. Readers interested in the history of women's education will find a landmark statement.
23686-the-life-and-adventures-of-poor-pu:
Lucy Gray wrote this mock memoir of a cat at Easingwold, in the manner of a serious life story told about a very unserious subject. Poor Puss was the favorite companion of Widow Wales and her little girl Julia. She died in her fifth year, after an internal disorder and shortness of breath, and was buried at the bottom of the garden.

Her life, as Gray relates it, began at a farmhouse, where she took early to petty thefts. She lapped cream from dairy bowls and stole meat from the table whenever she had a chance. Whippings made her shy of the dairy, but play with old Keeper the dog and hiding in his kennel kept her young life full. It is a gentle, funny elegy for a household pet.
23728-walter-and-the-wireless:
Sara Ware Bassett published Walter and the Wireless with Little, Brown in 1923, as one of her Invention Series for young readers. Companion volumes gave Paul the printing press, Steve the steam engine, and Ted the telephone. Walter's turn is radio, then still new enough to feel like magic.

Chapters follow Walter to a new job, his bow to his employer, the pursuit of Lola, a blunder and its results, and lessons in the laws of the air. The frontispiece catches a Chicago station, KYW, asking listeners to stand by for fifteen minutes. Bassett mixes a boy's working life with clear explanations of how wireless sends voices through the air.
23778-the-governess:
Julie M. Lippmann published The Governess in Toronto in 1916, though its copyright dates to 1897. Its heroine is Nan, a lively girl whose visitor, Mr. Turner's plan, and the arrival of a governess set the story moving. Charles R. Chickering's pictures show Nan standing her ground, running away, and sitting beside the little governess.

Chapters follow wheels within wheels, open confession, Nan's heroine, and having her own way, through Christmas, small clouds, and a sleigh-ride. Chester Newcomb appears late, and the book closes through deep waters toward another Christmas. It is a girls' story of home, discipline, and affection, in the manner of the period.
24293-christian-devotedness:
Anthony Norris Groves wrote this tract on the Savior's precept, lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth. Groves lived from 1795 to 1853, and the second edition appeared in London from James Nisbet in 1829. Before that edition appeared, Groves had taken the step his tract advocated, giving up earthly treasure for the work of faith. The tract reveals the spirit that made his ministry attractive to sincere souls.

In his preface, Groves says his views have not softened with four years. Daily experience has strengthened his trust in the deep knowledge of the human heart shown in the Lord's injunctions. The doctrine, received by faith, clears spiritual sight like eye-salve. Readers get a short, earnest call to hold wealth loosely and follow Christ fully.
24565-two-gallant-sons-of-devon-a-tale-o:
Harry Collingwood wrote this Elizabethan sea tale, opening at Devonport in June 1577, on a fair evening. Two young friends, after work, borrow a lugger from a boat-builder for a sail. A violent change of weather swamps their boat, and a passing privateer picks them up, refusing to waste time landing them.

Given places in the crew, the two fight a Spanish ship, take her goods, and release her, before sailing on to further adventures. Collingwood's tale mixes seamanship, privateering, and friendship into a brisk boys' adventure. Young readers get a stirring picture of Devon sailors in the days of Queen Bess.
24758-the-eyes-of-the-woods-a-story-of-t:
Joseph A. Altsheler published this frontier adventure in 1917, the fourth book in his Young Trailers series. Five young woodsmen, led by Henry Ware, flee through the swamps and forests of the old Ohio country with Shawnee trackers close behind them. The chase drives the plot from a flooded jungle to a hidden camp and a ring of buffalo.

Altsheler fills the story with woodcraft: reading tracks, hiding trails in water, and living off the land. The boys talk in rough frontier speech and lean on each other when danger closes in. Young readers get a fast-moving tale of the border wars, told with a strong feel for the woods themselves.
25170-facts-for-the-kind-hearted-of-engl:
Jasper W. Rogers's Facts for the Kind-Hearted of England, published in London in 1847, pleads for the wretched Irish peasantry and proposes means for their regeneration. The edition was sold at a ladies' bazaar to relieve famine in Ireland and distress in Scotland.

Rogers recalls his first arrival in London at the Swan with Two Necks, then turns to Ireland, where laborers lack work, land, and even lime to whitewash a cabin. He defends the poor man's pipe, his dhudeen, against charges of idleness. The pamphlet is both a famine appeal and a protest against English neglect.
25516-the-crown-of-success:
The Crown of Success is a moral tale for young readers, built around learning to read and the rewards of steady work. Early chapters follow a dame's departure, Mr. Learning at breakfast, the cottages of Head, and plain work beside fancy work.

Mr. Alphabet, Mr. Reading's fine shop, and the Ladder of Spelling turn lessons into characters and places a child can picture. A sparkling crown placed on a brow in one picture marks the goal. Success here means patient study, not sudden luck, and each setback teaches a fresh lesson to the reader. The author signs the tale A. L. O. E.
25678-on-the-old-road-vol-1-of-2-a-colle:
John Ruskin gathers miscellaneous essays and articles on art and literature in On the Old Road, volume one, covering 1834 to 1885, in the National Library Association edition of his complete works. Ruskin's monument, from a photograph, fronts the volume.

Contents treat Lord Lindsay's Christian Art, Eastlake's history of oil painting, and Samuel Prout, with Sir Joshua and Holbein. Pre-Raphaelitism, its principles and Turner, and its three colours follow. Architecture sections cover the Crystal Palace opening, study of architecture in schools, and an inaugural address at the Cambridge School of Art.
25689-the-secret-witness:
George Gibbs, author of Paradise Garden and The Yellow Dove, writes this 1917 spy novel, illustrated by George Brehm and published by Appleton. He dedicates it to Major R. Tait McKenzie of the Royal Army Medical Corps. A veiled figure, urged to hurry, fronts the book.

Contents open on 12 June 1914, with court secrets, the Habsburg haven, and secret information following. Two intruders, Herr Windt, and the green limousine lead to escape and capture, Captain Goritz, and diamond cuts diamond. The man in black, flight, tragedy, and the harim carry a wartime tale of secrets and witnesses.
25754-the-range-boss:
Charles Alden Seltzer, author of The Boss of the Lazy Y, writes The Range Boss, published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1916 with pictures by Frank E. Schoonover. Randerson watching newcomers fronts the book.

At Calamity Crossing opens the tale, as a rider climbs the shoulder of a mesa and halfway down a slope meets a sympathetic rescuer. At the Flying W, a memory of the rider, love versus business, and a man and his job follow. How an insult was avenged, what Uncle Jepson heard, and the law of the primitive carry a western story of range work and honour.
25859-the-telegraph-messenger-boy-or-the:
Edward S. Ellis tells how Ben, a poor country lad, climbs by grit, courtesy, and honest work. The tale opens on a log and a river collision, then moves to a telegraph office, where Ben carries messages through storm and dark. A night message, a cipher telegram, and a plot against a rich house test his nerve, while his rescue of Dolly the winter before wins him friends in high places.

First printed in 1889, the book takes its second title from its moral: the straight road to success runs through duty done well. Ben faces Farmer Jones, a grand house, a night affray, and rivals who lay low and watch. Each trial rewards the same traits, promptness, truth, and care for others, and the lad who began on a log ends with a fair place in the world.
25869-patty-s-success:
Carolyn Wells follows Patty home from a sea trip and into a busy winter of work and play. The book opens with a long, weary wait at the docks for the Mauretania, bringing her mother, Nan, Mr. Fairfield, and Patty herself. Christmas soon fills the house, with a splendid tree, skating, dancing, and ice cream shaped as trees, Santas, holly, bells, and mistletoe boughs.

Printed in 1910, the tale turns on Patty's pluck in trade: a fair offer leads to Department G, embroidered blossoms, slips and sleeves, three hats, and a clever goldfish of a scheme. The Thursday Club, Mrs. Van Reypen, and persistent Philip test her, but the road to success runs through honest work and good cheer. Christine's visit and a pleasing close round out the book.
25993-with-cochrane-the-dauntless:
G. A. Henty tells the exploits of Lord Cochrane in South American waters in With Cochrane the Dauntless, printed by Blackie in 1897 with pictures by W. H. Margetson. Henty's preface ranks Cochrane high among British sailors, likening him to the Earl of Peterborough in daring, genius for war, and love of adventure. Both did feats most men called impossible, and neither won full credit from his countrymen.

Cochrane spent his life fighting for the oppressed, Henty says, ruining his navy career by his crusade against naval abuses. Chapters run from the Malay archipelago to a dangerous companion and capture by Indians. One camp scene plans a creeper defense against sudden attack and a block and tackle to haul casks up a cliff. Henty writes of sea daring with his usual brisk pace.
26066-the-cosmic-express:
Jack Williamson tells a pulp tale of time travel and a strange machine in The Cosmic Express, from Amazing Stories, November 1930, reprinted in 1961. A lean man with a black bag darts from an elevator shaft into a little room cut by a high brass grill, like a depot waiting room. Behind the grill a lazy, brown eyed youth leans at a window, and beyond him glitters a great machine, half hid by brass.

The travelers must soon live like early folk: build a fire, find weapons, raise shelter, and seek a dry cave with skins to sleep on and pots to cook in. Flint comes first, for tools and sparks, with native copper likely near. Williamson writes of a cosmic train that drops its riders in a jungle past, where mud is plenty and savage beasts prowl.
261-a-dome-of-many-coloured-glass:
Amy Lowell's first book takes its title from Shelley's image of life staining eternity's light. A Dome of Many-Coloured Glass, from the 1912 edition in its third printing, gathers lyrical poems on art, travel, and feeling. Keats, Venetian glass, and Japanese carving inspire early pieces.

Later poems visit Dublin, Avignon, and New York at night, with color and craft in every line. Lowell's imagist eye favors sharp pictures over loose sentiment. The volume shows a poet learning her trade before her bolder work. It remains a lovely debut. Lowell's later imagist work grew from the careful pictures in this debut.
26136-the-worship-of-the-church-and-the-:
J. A. Regester, rector of St. Paul's Church in Buffalo, sets out the worship of the church and the beauty of holiness in this 1898 volume. It was revised for a second edition the same year. Chapters cover worship itself, the church as place of worship, the symbolism of the building, its arrangement and furniture, and its symbolic ornaments.

Regester explains the Trinity figure of a triangle ending in three circles, with a center circle joined to each. Its Latin legend names Deus, Pater, Filius, and Sanctus Spiritus, with est and non est. For the first four centuries, he notes, the Father was shown only as a hand issuing from clouds. The book teaches churchgoers to read their building as a symbol.
26283-the-huntress:
Hulbert Footner's 1922 novel The Huntress follows Bela, daughter of Charley Whitefish in a lakeside village. This photoplay edition ties to the First National picture with Colleen Moore and Lloyd Hughes. Bela is a firebrand and a scandal to her neighbours, a girl said to be born with the heart of a man. She refuses the place custom assigns her, and the village resents her for it.

Chapters promise advice from Musq'oosis, a visitor, dice that decide, suitors, a little meadow, and Bela's answer. Later scenes move to an island, a river, Johnny Gagnon's, and the Spirit River, where a man named Sam wakes to music drifting over water. The book mixes northern adventure with a romance of a wilful heroine.
26355-tom-the-bootblack-or-the-road-to-s:
Horatio Alger Jr. tells the story of Tom, a fifteen-year-old bootblack in New York who supports his weak grandfather Jacob from a poor tenement near City Hall. Tom earns small sums shining shoes and spends them on food for them both, starting one morning with thirty cents already earned for breakfast. His kindly neighbor Mrs. Flanagan cooks their eggs and coffee.

The novel follows the familiar Alger path from hard work and honest conduct toward a better life. Along the way Tom meets a well-dressed double, and he briefly enjoys posing as a gentleman named Gilbert, to the bewilderment of a fellow bootblack. Kindness, pluck, and steady effort carry him past sharper characters, including one who waves a forged paper in triumph.
26596-anna-the-adventuress:
E. Phillips Oppenheim published this London novel with Ward, Lock and Company, built on a double identity. Annabel Pellissier, for reasons of her own, lets Sir John Ferringhall believe she is her sister Anna. Anna then bears the burden of her sister's Paris reputation as a coquette, and endless complications follow when both sisters return to London.

The plot runs through a play called Alcide, with posters, hissing, and a change in its fortunes, plus a marriage certificate, a discomfited Sir John, and a case for the police. Nigel Ennison, Brendon, and Montague Hill puzzle over identification and truth. Anna's surrender and her sister's secret close a society thriller about sisters, reputation, and mistaken identity.
26661-the-power-of-darkness:
Leo Tolstoy wrote this drama in five acts in 1886, subtitled If a Claw Is Caught the Bird Is Lost. This hosted text presents the single play from his Plays Complete Edition, whose front matter sits in a companion volume. Its peasant household centers on Peter Ignatitch, a sickly, well-to-do peasant of forty-two, married a second time. His wife Anisya, thirty-two, fond of dress, and Akoulina, his daughter by his first marriage, complete the family.

Act One opens in autumn in a large village, in Peter's hut. Peter mends a horse-collar while Anisya and Akoulina spin and sing a part-song. Labourer Nikita, twenty-five, his God-fearing father Akim, and his mother Matryona complete the household, with orphan Marina, twenty-two, among the characters. Loose horses, scolding, and Matryona giving Anisya the powders set a household tragedy in motion.
26666-the-light-shines-in-darkness:
Leo Tolstoy's drama, in Louise and Aylmer Maude's translation, centers on Nicholas Ivánovich Sarýntsov and his family at a fine country house. Act one opens on the verandah, where children play croquet and Mary Ivánovna takes coffee with her sister Alexándra and brother-in-law Peter. Alexándra warns Mary that Nicholas is playing the fool and that, at the present rate, they will be beggared.

The cast widens far beyond the family, from peasants, priests, and a notary to generals, gendarmes, and doctors of a military asylum. Lyúba's betrothal, Ványa's tutor, and Princess Cheremshánov's children share the stage with soldiers and warders. Tolstoy stages a household divided by one man's convictions, and a world that answers idealism with law, medicine, and force.
2683-saint-s-progress:
John Galsworthy wrote this novel in four parts, opening on a July day when flags wave, poppies flame, and bees work the snapdragons under lime trees. A young woman's progress through love, war, and faith gives the book its title and its shape.

Galsworthy follows his saint through family pressure, a soldier's love, and the hard lessons of a nation at war. His prose is restrained, and his sympathy lies with those who try to live decently in indecent times. The novel stands as a wartime study of conscience, and of grace under strain.
26975-chapters-in-rural-progress:
Kenyon L. Butterfield, president of the Massachusetts Agricultural College, sets out his program for country life in Chapters in Rural Progress, published by the University of Chicago Press in 1908. The book treats the farm question as a social question, not only an economic one.

Its chapters cover farmers' institutes, the Hesperia movement, the rural school and the community, the Grange, and chances for farm women. Later chapters take up the country church, New England agriculture, and federation for rural progress, arguing that country towns must organize to thrive. Butterfield dedicated the book to his father, Ira Howard Butterfield, and the press issued a fifth impression in 1916.
2724-theodore-roosevelt-and-his-times-a-:
Harold Howland wrote this chronicle of Theodore Roosevelt and the progressive movement for the Chronicles of America series. The young fighter enters the New York Assembly, champions civil service reform, and earns the nickname Haroun al Roosevelt.

Fighting and breakfasting with Platt, becoming president, and dealing squarely with business follow, in chapters on the Square Deal for business and labor. Howland writes with admiration and clarity. The book serves as a brisk life of Roosevelt in his times, and of the movement he led. Howland keeps the narrative brisk and admiring throughout.
27505-winning-the-wilderness:
Margaret Hill McCarter, author of The Price of the Prairie and A Wall of Men, wrote this book of pioneer life, with illustrations by J. N. Marchand. Its opening poem, by Mrs. J. K. Hudson, asks who blazed the way to greater things, and answers with the man who dug the ground.

That man, the poem says, ended the long wandering of wild men and set the task of building human homes. With a stone axe made into a hoe, he planted vine and figtree at the door and made nations possible. The farmer, Hudson declares, is king. McCarter's book celebrates the pioneers who won the wilderness by farming it.
27834-paul-and-the-printing-press:
Sara Ware Bassett published Paul and the Printing Press with Little, Brown and Company of Boston in 1920, in her Invention Series, with illustrations by A. O. Scott. The story follows Paul Cameron, a boy inspired to start a monthly paper for his school.

Chapters follow a class meeting, a game of cards, a mad tea party, the romance of bookmaking, a pilgrimage to the city, and graduation. Bassett thanks the editor of the Boston Post for help, and the book teaches boys how printing works while telling an encouraging story of enterprise.
27930-david-fleming-s-forgiveness:
Margaret Murray Robertson wrote David Fleming's Forgiveness, a Canadian settlement novel opening with the two Holt brothers felling the first tree south and west of Hawk's Head. The brothers left a thickly settled New England valley, crossed mountains and forests, and squatted in a fertile Canadian valley known only to trappers and Indians.

Within ten years a village grew around Gershom Holt's sawmill on the Beaver River, with store, schoolhouse, and blacksmith's shop, and titles were later secured on easy terms. The novel follows settlement, prosperity, and forgiveness in the slow building of a Canadian community.
28000-inaugural-presidential-address:
This volume gathers several transcriptions of Barack Obama's inaugural presidential address, delivered from noon to 12:15 p.m. on January 20, 2009, as prepared by Project Gutenberg volunteers. The note explains that the official White House version appears in a companion e-book, number 28001, while this volume sticks to what was said.

One version was transcribed live by a team of volunteers and proofread several times; another is Michael Hart's own transcription, typed on a new computer. The address speaks of crisis, war, a weakened economy, and faithfulness to the founders' ideals, and the volume preserves the speech as heard, with pauses and applause marked.
28008-under-the-southern-cross:
Elizabeth Robins, author of The Magnetic North and The Open Question, published Under the Southern Cross with Frederick A. Stokes Company in October 1907, illustrated and decorated by John Rae. The book opens as a confession to her sisters, from a plain American girl of twenty who spent a winter in San Francisco.

Chapters follow an agreeable fellow passenger, an interpreter at Mazatlan, coconut milk and pearl fishing, a baron crazy with madness, and the Inca eye. Robins writes travel and romance with a feminist eye, and the volume preserves a woman traveler's view of Mexico and the Pacific.
28033-the-wild-huntress-love-in-the-wild:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote The Wild Huntress, love in the wilderness, first published in 1855 as his ninth book in the Wild West genre, in one hundred and five chapters of length. The story opens with Frank Wingrove, who bought Tennessee land already held by squatter Hickman Holt and came to set out his case.

Frank and the squatter are about to fight a duel when someone else steps in. Frank falls in reciprocated love with one of Holt's two beautiful daughters. The tale moves toward California, Indians, and a Mormon train bound for Salt Lake City, in Reid's masterly frontier manner.
28171-they-shall-not-pass:
Frank H. Simonds wrote They Shall Not Pass in 1916 from articles first printed in the New York Tribune. Simonds travelled to Verdun, met General Petain, and saw a city dying under shells, with houses vanishing hour by hour. He lunched underground, toasted America, and watched French soldiers hold a line they would not give up.

Later chapters compare Verdun to Gettysburg, calling the Crown Prince's attack the high tide of the German effort. Simonds writes as a war correspondent, vivid and partisan for France. The book gives American readers an early, close report of the longest battle of the First World War.
29167-secret-memoirs-the-story-of-louise:
Henry W. Fischer published this book in 1912, drawn from the diary of Louise, Crown Princess of Saxony, lost when she eloped from Dresden with Andre Giron. This edition, printed on Japanese vellum paper, was limited to two hundred and fifty copies. It covers the court of Royal Saxony from 1891 to 1902.

Chapters follow Louise's sweet family, a weeping willow as emblem royal, an unpleasant youth, and a fierce disciplinarian. Fischer, author of books on the courts of Berlin and William II, presents the diary as a window into a gilded, unhappy royal life. Readers get a scandalous royal memoir, part diary and part court history, about a princess who fled her throne for love.
29188-ebrietatis-encomium-or-the-praise-:
Albert-Henri de Sallengre first published this mock-praise of drunkenness in French in 1714 as Eloge de l'Yvresse. Robert Samber translated it into English in 1723 under the title Ebrietatis Encomium, or The Praise of Drunkenness, signed by the joking pen name Boniface Oinophilus, lover of wine. This text follows the 1812 edition.

Chapters argue, tongue in cheek, that one must be merry while living, that wine banishes sorrow and stirs mirth, and that getting drunk sometimes is good for health. Old people, the author claims, ought to drink sometimes, and wine creates wit and eloquence. Readers get a witty eighteenth-century satire, playful in form and learned in quotation, praising the bottle with a straight face.
29278-the-innocent-adventuress:
Mary Hastings Bradley published this novel in New York in 1921 with D. Appleton and Company, copyrighted in 1920 by the McCall Company. Bradley wrote The Fortieth Door and The Palace of Darkened Windows. She opens with an eavesdropper: Maria Angelina, listening in. Maria was assigned to chaperon her sister Lucia and Paolo Tosti by reading in the next room.

Later chapters bring undiscovered country, luncheon at the lodge, Ri-Ri singing again, and dances where two and a mountain meet. Johnny becomes inevitable, then explicit, Mrs. Blair regrets, and fantasy gives way to morning light. Readers get a romantic novel of manners and adventure, light in touch and Italian in setting, about a young woman listening her way into her own story.
29406-the-country-beyond-a-romance-of-th:
James Oliver Curwood published this romance of the wilderness, with a frontispiece showing a whispered promise: We'll make it, Peter. Curwood, author of The Valley of Silent Men and The Flaming Forest, sets his tale not far from the rugged, storm-whipped north shore of Lake Superior, south of the Kaministiqua. The story opens with a reflection on trivial things that change history: a glass of wine, a nail, a woman's smile.

Peter and Nada carry the romance, with children racing ahead to tell camp news and a message from Yellow Bird, a squaw, that visitors would be welcome. Readers get a northern wilderness romance, warm and adventurous, where love and loyalty are tested against a hard, beautiful country.
29421-the-floating-island-of-madness:
Jason Kirby published this story in Astounding Stories in January 1933. High over the Arabian Desert, three Secret Service men discover an aerial island of madmen. The narrator, flying with Paul Foulet of the French Surete and Douglas Brice of Scotland Yard, follows a tiny speck eastward from dawn to sunset.

Below stretches the tawny waste of the desert under a pale, hot, cloudless sky. The flyers debate whether to go on or turn back, how long gas and oil will hold, and just where they are. Brice shouts too fast above the motors. Readers get a pulp adventure of international detectives and a floating island, where the madness above the desert is the mystery itself.
29552-the-temple-of-glass:
John Lydgate's Temple of Glass, printed at Westminster by William Caxton about 1477, survives in this 1905 Cambridge facsimile reprint. The unique book came to Cambridge University Library within a famous volume of tracts once owned by John Moore, Bishop of Ely. It reached the university as a gift from King George the First in 1715. The printer certifies only 250 copies, with plates rubbed off and negatives destroyed.

Lydgate's poem opens in Middle English, with the speaker stunned by light as he nears a grisly, dreadful place, bright as crystal and nearer and nearer. The temple of glass becomes a dream vision of love and fate. Readers of medieval verse will find a rare, beautiful survival from the first age of English print.
29673-creating-capital-money-making-as-a:
Frederick L. Lipman wrote Creating Capital: Money-Making as an Aim in Business, a Barbara Weinstock Lecture on the Morals of Trade, printed in 1918 by Houghton Mifflin. Lipman opens with the typical money-maker as commonly pictured: a narrow, grasping, selfish figure who has chosen lower rather than higher ideals. His lecture asks whether that picture is fair, and what money-making can mean when pursued as a worthy aim.

The book argues that creating capital, rightly understood, serves more than the maker. It belongs to a series on the moral law in business life under a new economic order. Students of business ethics will find a thoughtful, period defense of enterprise with a conscience.
3-john-f-kennedy-s-inaugural-address:
A new president spoke at noon on a cold January day in 1961. John F. Kennedy framed his inaugural address as a handover to a generation born in the twentieth century. He pledged American support for liberty abroad, at any price and burden.

The speech asks citizens to serve their country rather than ask what it can do for them. Allies get loyalty, adversaries get a warning, and the United Nations gets a plea for peace. Its short lines on duty and sacrifice made it one of the most quoted speeches in American history.
30074-jessica-the-heiress:
Evelyn Raymond wrote Jessica, the Heiress, printed in Racine, Wisconsin, in 1904 by the Whitman Publishing Company, with copyright held by the Federal Book Company. Raymond had already written Jessica Trent and Jessica Trent's Inheritance. Twenty-one chapters carry the story, from Jessica disappears and the hush of anxiety through Old Century takes the trail, deliverance, and Jessica's story, to behind locked doors. A royal gift and the face at the window follow.

The prisoner disappears, the road home opens, Old Century passes, and the lads rebel. Ned's story, the doctor's advice, Ninian's greeting, and Jessica gets her wish follow, with the cactus hedge, what the Sabbath brought, Antonio's confession, and the verdict. Chapter one opens on the south porch of the Sobrante ranch house. Mrs. Benton sews as fast as she rocks and talks faster than either, while Jessica swings in her hammock among roses, fuchsias, calla lilies, and poinsettia.
30189-show-business:
Boyd Ellanby tells a Mars show-business tale from Luna City, with pictures by Mel Hunter, in a short piece on a promoter of Martian dancing girls, vaudeville, and other things. The narrator drops into Kotha's bar shortly after midnight to find it deserted except old Dworken, a Venusian friend with heavy green lids and a tail. An Earth ship stays two days away, while a Martian flagship due next morning will carry seven hundred passengers home.

Dworken, waiting a whole week at six thousand credits a day, orders another shchikh and invites the narrator to drink, though tomorrow brings the first tourist crowd of the season. Six explosive drinks already stand empty before him, yet he shows no effect. The humor lies in the gap between a promoter's easy money and a working man's dread of the mob to come.
30302-the-benefactress:
The author of Elizabeth and Her German Garden tells of Anna Estcourt, a pretty girl of twenty-five who wonders whether life's pleasure balances its bother, in a Macmillan volume from 1901. Anna's face is soft and irregular, her eyes charming, her laugh pleasant, with dimples and long, slender limbs, and by all rights ought to be enjoying herself. Instead she wastes time pondering puzzles of existence, those unanswerable whys and wherefores usually left, the narrator says, to the elderly and plain.

Her motive is no loftier than a sister-in-law's perpetual presence, rich in itself a pleasing fact, but also frank, while Anna and her husband depend on her entirely. Richness and frankness together make the sister-in-law's visits fatiguingly frequent, and a wonderful thing then happens to Anna. The novel promises wit, money, and a young woman's search for a life of her own.
30394-dave-porter-and-his-double-or-the-:
Edward Stratemeyer tells Dave Porter and His Double, or The Disappearance of the Basswood Fortune, published in Boston by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard in August 1916, illustrated by Walter S. Rogers. Stratemeyer, author of Dave Porter at Oak Hall and the Old Glory, Colonial, Pan-American, and Soldiers of Fortune series, opens off for a sleigh-ride. Something of the past, a team that ran away, and Ward Porton again follow.

What Asa Dickley had to say, more trouble, and face to face follow, with the Basswood fortune, something about miniatures, a big sleighing-party, and a hold by the blizzard. Tim Crapsey's plot, what Washington Bones had to tell, movements of the enemy, and the return to Crumville carry the tale. How the miniatures disappeared, a vain search, a civil engineering examination, and off for Texas follow. An illustration shows a team crashing through a frail rail-fence.
30398-the-other-likeness:
James H. Schmitz opens a science fiction tale with Dr. Halder Leorm, who feels a sharp tingling from an alarm device under his wrist watch while studying a culture tray. He slips the device from his wrist, removes its back plate, and views his distant home in another district of Draise, a great city of Orado.

On the carpet lies a man on his back, eyes shut, face deeply flushed, apparently unconscious: Dr. Atteo, newly assigned to his laboratory that week. Beyond Atteo, an entry from the delivery area and car port hints at how he arrived. Schmitz frames a puzzle of likeness and counterfeit, where perfection itself may carry an odd effect.
30435-a-book-of-sibyls-miss-barbauld-mis:
Miss Thackeray, Mrs. Richmond Ritchie, writes A Book of Sibyls, published in London in 1883 and reprinted from the Cornhill Magazine. Four sibyls give the book its frame: Mrs. Barbauld, Miss Edgeworth, Mrs. Opie, and Miss Austen, dedicated in spirit to Mrs. Oliphant, a sibyl of the author's own day.

A preface opens at a London luncheon, where friends debate the county of Maple Grove and the allusion to Selina, while a French guest misses the reference. Thackeray uses that scene to introduce women writers as prophetesses of domestic life. The book blends memoir, criticism, and affection into portraits of four influential women authors.
3048-the-little-duke-richard-the-fearles:
Charlotte Yonge wrote The Little Duke: Richard the Fearless for young readers, first published for Macmillan in 1864 and reprinted many times through 1901. The title page names the author only as the author of The Heir of Redclyffe, Yonge's famous novel, a common practice of the day. The story follows Richard, the boy duke of Normandy, through plots, captivity, and rescue. Scenes turn on loyalty and cunning, as Sir Eric tests a young Frenchman.

Osmond begs never to be called young Frenchman again, and a drawbridge, an ivy branch, and a secret message decide a castle's fate. Yonge's history stays close to the chronicles while shaping them for children. The book remains a classic introduction to Norman history for young readers.
30728-oneness:
James H. Schmitz wrote this science fiction story, printed in Analog in May 1963, about a trial that could hand Earth a star drive. Sixty years earlier, carelessness cost Earth its first chance at a true interstellar drive. Now directors of the Machine, the political body that has run Earth for a century and a half, gather in a vast Tribunal Hall to learn its secrets from a prisoner.

Menesee, one of the directors, takes his box between Cornelius and Ojeda, near the Spokesman's Platform, and studies the prisoner as Administrator Bradshaw and Spokesman Dorn take their places. The story turns on a moral weapon: a power that could force people to live by the Golden Rule. Schmitz asks whether such a power would save humanity or enslave it, and who should hold it.
30968-a-sunny-little-lass:
Evelyn Raymond wrote this 1906 children's book, published by Hurst and Company in New York, with copyright held by George W. Jacobs and Company. Its thirteen chapters run from The One Room House and After the Colonel's Visit through In Elbow Lane, Beside Old Trinity, and A Desolate Awakening. They continue with The Beginning of the Search, A Guardian Angel, With Bonny as Guide, and In the Ferry-House.

Later chapters bring Another Stage of the Journey, A Haven of Refuge, News from the Lane, and The Wonderful Ending. The book opens in the littlest house in New York, where Glory lives with grandpa and Bo'sn the dog. It is a piece-of-pie shaped little room built to use a scant narrow triangular space between two big warehouses. It is a sunny, old-fashioned tale of a little girl in the city.
3121-thoughts-suggested-by-mr-froude-s-p:
Warner starts from a wish many men voice: to return to earth ages after leaving it. Some would trade months or years of life for a shorter span on the globe two or three centuries hence. Merely watching from afar, like a spectator at a play in dumb show, would not satisfy them. They want to live in the world again and take part in its affairs.

Froude's writing on progress prompts the musing. Warner turns it into a question about change itself: what would a returned traveler recognize, and what would baffle him? The essay is a gentle piece of speculation, less about prophecy than about how fast habits, faith, and daily life may shift while human nature stays much the same.
3132-in-the-wilderness:
Warner gathers his Adirondack pieces in this volume. He opens with a plain account of killing a bear, since conflicting stories had already spread. The meeting was unplanned on both sides, he insists. As he seldom has occasion to kill a bear, the exploit may be excused a celebration. A fight with a trout and a deer hunt follow, plus a study of the guide Old Phelps.

Getting lost, camping out, and a wilderness romance round out the set. Humor mixes with close watching of forest life throughout. The voice is the book's charm: a city man in the woods, honest about his blunders and fond of his guides.
31494-the-young-man-in-business:
Edward Bok's The Young Man in Business, part of the Day's Work Series and published by L. C. Page and Company of Boston in 1900, the year given as MDCCCC, is a short book of practical advice. It opens with a well-known New York millionaire's opinion. He held that health and fair intelligence could make a young man rich. Bok notes the statement was criticized, literally picked to pieces, and finally adjudged in various ways.

Bok, who knew business life from the inside, answers with plain counsel on work, character, and opportunity. The book speaks to young men starting out, urging steady habits over quick schemes. As a document of its age, it shows the gospel of success at its most earnest, and the doubts that already surrounded it.
31499-a-campfire-girl-s-happiness:
Jane L. Stewart's A Campfire Girl's Happiness is volume six of the Campfire Girls series. It was published by the Saalfield Publishing Company of Akron, Ohio, and New York, with copyright in 1914, the year given as MCMXIV. An illustration shows the girls with hearty appetites for the camp breakfast, a small, telling detail of camp life. Stewart follows her Camp Fire Girls through the season's activities, where council fires, hikes, and friendships shape the girls' growth.

The happiness of the title is the quiet reward of camp life well lived: health, companionship, and work done together. Stewart writes for girls in the Camp Fire tradition, with an emphasis on outdoor life and character. Readers of girls' series fiction will find a wholesome, old-fashioned volume, where the camp itself teaches its lessons.
31780-journal-of-a-trip-to-california-by:
E. S. Ingalls's journal, printed at Waukegan in 1852, records a trip to California by the overland route across the plains in 1850 and 1851. Ingalls disclaims any pretense to authorship, offering instead a plain, off-hand statement of incidents as he saw them, for friends and for others about to start for Eldorado.

The party set out from Lake County, Illinois, late in March, and the day-by-day entries follow roads, camps, and travelers on the long overland trail. Readers get a firsthand gold-rush diary, unpolished but direct, useful for the practical detail of a journey that many readers of 1852 hoped to make themselves.
31920-the-next-step-in-religion-an-essay:
Roy Wood Sellars's 1918 essay The Next Step in Religion, an essay toward the coming renaissance, was published by Macmillan. Its claim is that a fresh outlook on the universe and man's place within it is taking shape. It grows, Sellars says, in laboratories, studies, congresses of social workers, assemblies of reformers, studios of artists, and quietly in many homes.

Chapters move from the age of myth and stories of creation through magic and ritual, the origins of Christianity, the prophet of Nazareth, and the evolution of Christianity. Readers get a liberal philosophical essay that treats inherited belief as a bud's covering, slowly pushed aside by a view with more contact with living needs.
32148-international-incidents-for-discus:
L. Oppenheim, Whewell Professor of International Law at Cambridge, wrote this textbook for conversation classes, published by Cambridge University Press in 1909. Its method is simple: short international incidents, stated as cases, give language students something concrete to discuss. The incidents draw on diplomacy, war, and trade, turning points of international law into classroom talk.

Early sections cover a councillor of legation in difficulties, neutral goods on an enemy merchantman, American coasting trade, and a German balloon at Antwerp. Later items take up the use of the white flag and South American questions. Readers get a teaching book that doubles as a compact casebook. Each incident poses a legal problem in a few lines, inviting argument about what states may do and what they may not.
32226-the-flower-princess:
Abbie Farwell Brown's The Flower Princess, illustrated and published for children, gathers four fairy tales: The Flower Princess, The Little Friend, The Mermaid's Child, and The Ten Blowers.
