Brown, also author of The Curious Book of Birds, A Pocketful of Posies, and In the Days of Giants, writes in the classic fairy-tale manner. Its illustrations include a frontispiece captioned Let Him Prove It.

The title tale opens once upon a time with a beautiful Princess named Fleurette. She lives in a white marble palace on a high hill. Fond of flowers, she keeps a fair garden of wonderful plants. It slopes from the palace gates to the foot of the hill, snugly enclosed by a high marble wall. The hill rises like a great nosegay in the midst of the land. Readers get gentle, garden-filled fairy tales for young children.
32339-brink-of-madness:
Walt Sheldon's short story, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in July 1953, follows a criminological agent who trusts hunches over computers. Its sidenote credits C.I.B. Agent Pell with brains, though gut feel guides him more than any machine. When stakes turned rough, he learned that thinking well meant first staying alive. The first chapter opens on the night the visitors came, with Richard Pell working late among banks of computers.

Pell whistles off key, not caring, while Ciel, his wife, stays in his mind's eye, seen on the viewer minutes before. Be home shortly, baby, he says, as soon as he fills in a form or two, and she answers with slight doubt. It is a night, at once their second anniversary, and the start of a second honeymoon. Readers get a crime story, where hunches beat machines.
32784-the-dark-goddess:
Richard S. Shaver tells of a great mer-woman in deep caverns, in this story from Imagination Stories of Science and Fantasy of February 1953. From black-emerald water rises a vast and beautiful head, with hair that ripples with a life of its own, webbed fingers, and a tail where legs should be.

Her people, drawn from many human races of several near-forgotten planets, live tier on tier in a cavern city of bedrock. Their wandering planet now nears two great suns, and surface ice already melts into seas. Long alone, the goddess welcomed the first voyagers and taught them wisdom. Then comes McCarthy, a voyager from space, also lonely, and her laughter rings like a bell beneath water.
32917-the-sapphire-cross:
This fen-land romance opens with two young women walking the wild marshes, glad to escape London smoke, seaside promenades, and polite small talk. Marion, tall and pale, picks her way across tufts of heath and rushes, gathering moss and forget-me-nots, while her bright companion Ada teases her about running and jumping in the bogs. Beneath their talk lies a shared grief for Philip, whose dried bouquet Marion still keeps.

The sapphire cross of the title soon becomes the focus of mystery and longing, as Sir Murray demands to know where it has gone and old sorrows resurface. Set among pines, black water, and ancient roots dragged from the bog, the story mixes love, loss, and a missing jewel. It is a Victorian tale of feeling and suspense, rooted in the strange beauty of the fens.
33061-clover-and-blue-grass:
Eliza Calvert Hall's Clover and Blue Grass, published in Boston in 1916, is the last book of Aunt Jane stories, gathering tales of Kentucky country life. Its contents include How Parson Page Went to the Circus, the nineteenth and last Aunt Jane story, first printed in the Cosmopolitan. The rest includes Mary Crawford's Chart, Old Mahogany, Millstones and Stumbling-Blocks, One Taste of the Old Time, and One Day in Spring. A frontispiece shows a son thanking a mother for her daughter.

Hall, also author of Aunt Jane of Kentucky and The Land of Long Ago, writes in a voice that mixes humor, memory, and moral sense. Old women, parsons, and neighbors carry the wisdom of a place. The stories celebrate hand-woven coverlets, old furniture, and the talk of a Kentucky household. They remain a gentle, affectionate portrait of a rural world that was already passing when Hall wrote.
33446-lace-curtain-cleaning-a-successful:
Mrs. Albert Leigh's Lace Curtain Cleaning, a Successful Home Business, copyrighted in 1913, teaches how she started a thriving home trade. Leigh tells readers to begin at the beginning, read carefully to the end, and then begin work, with valuable instructions for those who applied for them. Her advice is for the reader's own use, not to be lent, if the reader wishes to succeed.

The book suits readers of home business and women's work history, offering a complete, practical guide to a niche trade. Its tone is plain and encouraging, from a woman who did the work herself. For those curious about early home businesses, it is a clear, useful manual, full of the details that turned clean curtains into cash.
33519-the-nest-the-white-pagoda-the-suic:
Anne Douglas Sedgwick gathers five stories of conscience, art, and mortality in this 1913 Century volume. The Nest opens with a man leaving a London specialist's door after learning he has only a month or two to live. He then takes a train to the country, while ordinary sights crowd in on him with new force. The White Pagoda, The Suicide, A Forsaken Temple, and Miss Jones and the Masterpiece complete the set.

Sedgwick writes with psychological precision about people facing death, disappointment, and the demands of work they admire. Her characters weigh what a shortened life, a ruined hope, or an artistic ambition should change in how they treat others. The collection suits readers who enjoy early twentieth-century stories of manners with a serious moral undertow.
3388-the-man-of-letters-as-a-man-of-busi:
William Dean Howells reflects on authorship as a trade in this essay from Literature and Life. A bibliographical note opens it with a doubt the writer owns himself. Howells admits readers may miss the inward unity he himself senses in these pieces. They look for all the world like scattered sketches and essays with no visible link between them.

No superficial allegiance joins them, he concedes, yet a common theme does: the writer as a working man, paid, delayed, and bargained with. Howells accounts plainly and honestly for living by the pen without ceasing to be a man of letters.
34029-parturition-without-pain-or-loss-o:
James Townley was a member of the Royal College of Physicians of Edinburgh and a fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons of England. He wrote this short medical work, in a second edition published in London in 1862. Townley argues for a new mode of giving an anodyne in childbirth, so that pain is eased without loss of consciousness.

Common chloroform, he says, goes slowly round the circulation before it acts, while his plan uses rapidly repeated, broken impressions on the nervous system to a different effect. A second edition within a few months showed that his views had drawn notice. The book gives a period view of early anaesthesia.
34092-dress-as-a-fine-art-with-suggestio:
Mary Philadelphia Merrifield's guide treats dress as an art governed by taste, fitness, and economy rather than passing fashion. Opening chapters survey head-dresses from past ages, then take up the head, the dress, and the feet in turn, with plates showing each style.

Later chapters judge single costumes, weigh ornament against cost, and close with plain advice on children's dress. The book suits readers who want sound rules for looking well without waste, drawn from old styles and from daily wear. Plates throughout show the styles described, so readers can match each rule to its image.
34180-the-exploits-and-triumphs-in-europ:
Paul Morphy's late secretary wrote this record of the chess champion's exploits and triumphs in Europe, published in New York in 1859 by D. Appleton and Company, illustrated with ten portraits on wood engraved by the Dalziel brothers. The book adds a historical account of clubs, biographical sketches of famous players, and anecdote on the noble game of chess.

A preface thanks George Walker, veteran chess-player, for most of the fourth chapter's information, with thanks also to Lowenthal, George Medley of the London Chess Club, and Ries of the Divan. Morphy's record is dedicated to the First American Chess Congress. The book offers a classic chess biography.
3485-annajanska-the-bolshevik-empress:
George Bernard Shaw writes a short play, first made as a twenty minute sketch for the variety stage, about a Russian grand duchess turned revolutionary. The action sits around a long table set for a general's inquiry, with a comfortable chair at one end and a plain bench at the other. Annajanska, once an empress in title, now faces soldiers and officials of the new order.

Shaw uses the sketch for wit and argument about revolution, rank, and power. His heroine refuses to beg or to apologize, and the comedy comes from her clash with men who expect obedience. The play suits readers who enjoy Shaw in brief form: sharp talk, a bold woman at the center, and politics turned into theater.
3658-the-prospector-a-tale-of-the-crow-s:
Ralph Connor writes a tale of the Crow's Nest Pass in the Canadian Rockies, where prospectors, railway men, and settlers meet. The chapters run from A Social Impossibility and Varsity versus McGill through The Voice in the Wilderness and Only One Claim. They continue with On the Trail, The Outpost, The Old Prospector, Tim Carroll, and Betty's Last Words. A young man from the east learns the West through work and hardship.

Connor, a minister and novelist, mixes adventure with moral appeal, praising courage, loyalty, and faith on the frontier. The prospector himself, old and weathered, guides the younger men. The book suits readers who enjoy Canadian frontier fiction, with mountains, mines, and a romance at its heart.
4286-mastery-of-self-for-wealth-power-su:
Frank Channing Haddock wrote this self-help book on the power of self-mastery as a road to wealth, power, and success. Its chapters treat will, habit, and the training of thought, urging readers to govern their own minds before they try to govern their affairs. The tone is confident and practical, in the manner of early twentieth-century success literature.

Haddock offers exercises and maxims rather than a system of business advice. He argues that character, rightly drilled, produces outward results. Modern readers may find the claims dated, but the book remains a clear sample of the period's faith in mind power and personal discipline.
4353-five-thousand-an-hour-how-johnny-ga:
George Randolph Chester wrote this comic business novel around Johnny Gamble, a promoter down to his last hundred dollars. The contents introduce Johnny, make strangers into old friends, mix business with pleasure, and show Johnny's talent as a true promoter. Later chapters bring a magnificent twenty-story hotel dream and Constance's growing interest.

Chester, author of Get-Rich-Quick Wallingford, writes fast, slangy American business comedy. Johnny gambles on schemes, talk, and nerve, aiming at five thousand an hour and at the heiress herself. The novel is light entertainment of the go-getter age, with a hero whose chief capital is confidence.
4603-in-the-wilderness:
Robert Hichens opens this novel in Milan in the autumn of 1894, at the Hotel Cavour, where hall porter Amedeo Dorini waits for the station omnibus. Amedeo, a shrewd student of human nature, judges travellers by their luggage, their manner, and their tips, and he has a horror of tin trunks. His watchful eye sets the tone for a story about people observed, weighed, and often misjudged.

The book is divided into larger movements, beginning with Hermes and the Child and continuing with Echo and later books. Hichens follows his characters through hotels, journeys, and lonely places, where desire, duty, and faith pull against each other. Readers get a slow, atmospheric novel of character, written by a novelist who liked grand settings and the quiet drama of a life changed by a single meeting.
462-the-errand-boy-or-how-phil-brent-won:
Horatio Alger Jr. follows Phil Brent, a boy bullied by a stepbrother, in this success tale. Phil, plodding home through snow, takes a snowball to the ear and chases his tormentor Jonas across the fields. That small fight opens a longer road of jobs, tricks, and rivals in town and shop.

Alger adds two shorter tales, Fred Sargent's revenge and the smuggler's trap, to the volume. Phil wins by pluck, honesty, and hard work, the Alger formula at its plainest. Young readers will find a brisk, hopeful story where a good boy outlasts sly foes and earns his place.
4625-lizzy-glenn-or-the-trials-of-a-seam:
T. S. Arthur published Lizzy Glenn, or The Trials of a Seamstress, at Philadelphia in 1859, and he sets Hood's Song of the Shirt at its head. The verses speak of work till the brain swims and the eyes grow dim. They name seam and gusset and band, till the sewer falls asleep over her buttons and sews them in a dream. Lizzy Glenn, a needlewoman, lives that life, through Mrs. Gaston's sick child and a mother's anguish.

Later chapters follow how a needlewoman lives, the troubles of her trade, a friend in need, and Perkins' narrative. Henry Gaston leaves home with Sharp and suffers harsh treatment, while Lizzy finds an old friend in Mrs. Gaston and tells her own story. Perkins at last finds in Lizzy his long-lost Eugenia. Readers get a sympathetic Victorian tale about women's work, poverty, and recognition, told with Arthur's plain moral force.
4634-uncle-william-the-man-who-was-shif-:
Jennette Lee tells Uncle William, the Man Who Was Shif'less, opening with William Benslow's cheerful confession. Yes, he says, I am shif'less, and generally considered shif'less, speaking in a tone of satisfaction as he hitches his trousers into place by their one suspender. His companion shifts an easel, squinting across the harbour at changing light, where a mysterious green in the water fails to appear in his colour-box.

William watches patiently, and asks whether painting is not kind of ticklish business. The artist admits it is, and the old man says he reckons he would never have done for a painter, since it is sitting work. From that harbour meeting grows a story of an easy-going old man, an artist, and a coastal town. Readers get a warm, humorous novel about idleness, kindness, and the value of a life lived at its own pace.
4671-the-story-of-the-pony-express:
Glenn D. Bradley wrote The Story of the Pony Express as an account of the most remarkable mail service ever in existence, and its place in history. His preface states one purpose: to give an authentic, useful, and readable account of the enterprise. The Pony Express, he says, played an important part in history, and showed what American spirit can accomplish, though little formal writing on it existed.

Bradley covers inception, organisation, development, historical background, and anecdotes from its operation. He notes that the heroes of sixty-one were not all south of the Mason-Dixon line fighting each other, and he draws on a wide, fragmentary range of material. Readers get a short, lively history of riders, stations, and swift mail across the plains, for young readers and for anyone who loves western adventure.
4743-the-country-beyond-a-romance-of-the:
James Oliver Curwood sets The Country Beyond not far from the rugged, storm-whipped north shore of Lake Superior, south of the Kaministiqua and not as far south as the Rainy River waterway. There, he says, lay a paradise lost, and a frontispiece whispers, We'll make it, Peter. Illustrations promise a squaw named Yellow Bird, children racing with news, and a heroine confessing she has been living a lie.

Curwood notes how trivial things change lives: a glass of wine once lost a kingdom, a nail turned a mighty battle, and a woman's smile once destroyed a million homes. Peter, his hero, does not yet know such lessons. Readers get a northern wilderness romance of love, flight, and new country, with lakes, forests, and frontier settlements, in Curwood's vivid, popular style.
5064-the-voyage-of-the-hoppergrass:
The Voyage of the Hoppergrass begins luckily, because the boat is large. Only four set out, counting Captain Bannister. The party keeps picking up unexpected passengers. Soon the captain jokes they will have the whole county aboard. Everyone is glad before coming home of a comfortable cabin with plenty of sleeping room.

The Hoppergrass is a big white cat-boat, her name in gilt letters on her stern. She lies at anchor well out toward the middle of the river at five on a July morning. The catalog record leaves the author unnamed. Readers get a river voyage tale of growing company and small adventures, told with summer-morning freshness.
5265-the-ball-and-the-cross:
G. K. Chesterton's Ball and the Cross opens with a discussion somewhat in the air, aboard the flying ship of Professor Lucifer. It sets a Catholic Highlander, Evan MacIan, against an atheist journalist, James Turnbull. The two agree to fight a duel over religion, and the world, in the form of police, doctors, and peacemakers, keeps stopping them.

Chapters carry the duel to a village, a desert island, a garden of peace. A museum of souls follows, with dreams of MacIan and of Turnbull along the way. Chesterton turns a philosophical argument into a fantasy adventure, and the novel remains his most original defence of faith as a thing worth fighting for.
553-out-of-time-s-abyss:
Edgar Rice Burroughs follows Bradley after he leaves Fort Dinosaur in this Caspak tale, third in the series. On 4 September 1916, Bradley and four mates march from the great lake toward barrier cliffs, seeking a way to scale them. Jungles, eucalyptus forests, and giant ferns hide beasts at every turn.

Burroughs writes fast, vivid adventure, with rifles seldom cool and jokes traded under threat. A growl from a thicket ends the opening march. The book closes the Caspak arc with a lost explorer's fight through a land where time itself seems to run backward.
5898-jess:
Rider Haggard sets Jess in South Africa, opening with John having an adventure and sisters coming to Mooifontein. Chapters introduce Mr Frank Muller, Bessie asked in marriage, dreams dismissed as foolishness, and the storm breaking over love's young dream. Jess then goes to Pretoria, with Jantje and further trials ahead, as Boer and British tensions shape private lives.

The volume offers a romance of the Transvaal frontier, where love, loyalty, and political storm intertwine. Haggard writes with adventure energy, letting farm, town, and veldt carry the plot. The novel suits fans of Haggard beyond his lost-world tales, and readers who enjoy historical romance set in southern Africa before the Boer War.
5994-our-nervous-friends-illustrating-th:
Robert S. Carroll, medical director of Highland Hospital at Asheville, writes about nerves as friends that can be trained. His chapters move from friendly nerves and the neurotic, through the price of nervousness and the wrecking of a generation, to the nervously damaged mother and the child wrongly started.

Later sections treat eating errors, the crime of inactivity, learning to eat, the therapy of work, and the fine art of play. Carroll argues that diet, work, and recreation can retrain misdirected energy. The book speaks to readers who feel frayed, offering plain counsel instead of mystery.
6101-the-nature-of-goodness:
George Herbert Palmer, Alford Professor of Philosophy at Harvard, delivered The Nature of Goodness as lectures at Harvard, Dartmouth, Wellesley, Western Reserve, California, and Boston's Twentieth Century Club. Part of the sixth chapter served as a Phi Beta Kappa address, another part before Berkeley's Philosophical Union.

Audiences aided his work with searching criticism, clearing his thought and simplifying expression. Since discussions so severe felt vital to companies so diverse, Palmer offers them to a wider audience. Following his Field of Ethics, he asks what goodness is, how it is known, and why it binds us.
6657-the-theology-of-holiness:
Dougan Clark, professor at Earlham College, sets out the theology of holiness as taught in the Friends' church. Clark dedicates the book to his parents, both long-approved Friends ministers. It moves from entire sanctification as a need and as a gift. Then it runs through patriarchs, types, and prophecy to the teaching of Jesus, Paul, Peter, John, James, and Jude.

Clark writes with a teacher's order and a believer's warmth, grounding each claim in scripture. His aim is not debate for its own sake, but a life made holy by God. The Theology of Holiness is a clear, earnest statement of Quaker doctrine, useful to students of American religious thought.
697-the-light-princess:
George MacDonald wrote this fairy tale about a princess cursed at birth to lose her gravity: she floats, laughs at all sorrow, and cannot feel weight or grief. Her parents seek cures, from wise men to water, while a prince from a neighbouring realm learns her plight. The tale is told with wit and a light, teasing tone.

The cure comes only through love and loss, when the princess must choose feeling over ease. MacDonald uses the fancy to ask what a life without sorrow would lack, and what it costs to grow a heart. Loved by children for its jokes and by adults for its depth, it stands among the finest Victorian fairy tales.
6976-metlakahtla-and-the-north-pacific-m:
This little book tells of Metlakahtla, the North Pacific mission of the Church Missionary Society, with a map. A Psalm verse at its head speaks of taking the wings of the morning to the uttermost parts of the sea. A hymn calls the shores of the utmost west to break into song for the Crucified. The note explains that chapters three, four, and five reprint parts of an 1868 pamphlet. That pamphlet told of ten years work among the Tsimshean Indians.

Almost all the rest is new in separate form, though much had appeared in the Society's periodicals. One or two facts come from Halcombe's writings on the mission. The book records a mission community on the far Pacific coast, its schools, worship, and daily life, as seen by those who built it.
7052-dr-heidenhoff-s-process:
Edward Bellamy's Doctor Heidenhoff's Process opens in a Newville prayer meeting room, where a clock over a card reading Stand Up for Jesus points to ten minutes to nine. Cards reading Come Unto Me and The Wonderful, the Counsellor flank it, and a long pause follows the usual parts. Newville meetings divide attendants strictly into speakers and listeners, except in revivals or times of special interest.

Deacon Tuttle has spoken and prayed, Deacon Miller has prayed and spoken, Brother Hunt has enlarged a sermon point, and Brother Taylor has called attention to a matter. Into this ordered piety comes Heidenhoff's strange process, promising relief from a burdened conscience. Bellamy turns a small town meeting into a tale of guilt, memory, and science.
7059-peregrine-s-progress:
Jeffery Farnol sends Peregrine on his progress in a romance headed by a motto on imagination as a fearful magic, scaling heaven or plumbing hell. The contents open with an ante scriptum and a first book of silent places, introducing the hero and telling how and why he set forth on his quest. An extraordinary tinker, a down at heels gentleman named Anthony, and lively happenings at the Jolly Waggoner inn follow.

White magic, a forlorn parting, and the woes of Galloping Jerry the highwayman lead to philosophy, proof that clothes make the man, and the price of a goddess. The hero learns his own cowardice, finds a goddess wholly feminine, and begins to appreciate his fortune. Farnol writes a high spirited Georgian adventure of road, inn, and love.
724-the-man-of-letters-as-a-man-of-busin:
William Dean Howells argued in this essay that every writer ought to earn a living by work, and that art alone should not be a trade. He holds that a writer who has proven his fitness and earned his bread may then give his art freely. Society, he adds, should see to it that honest work brings a living wage.

Howells writes against the romantic view of the starving artist and the market view of books as mere goods. His tone is plain, humane, and practical. The essay still speaks to writers who must balance craft and cash, and it shows Howells, the dean of American letters, thinking hard about the place of authors in a business age.
7448-the-hour-glass:
W. B. Yeats called The Hour-Glass a morality, a play about the choices that shape a soul. Its persons are a Wise Man, a Fool, some pupils, an Angel, the Wise Man's wife, and two children. The scene is a large room with a desk, benches, and an hourglass on a bracket by the door. The Wise Man sits turning the pages of a book for his pupils' lesson.

The book quotes a beggar's writing on the walls of Babylon: there are two living countries, the one visible and the one invisible. The play tests what happens when a man who trusts only the visible world meets the other country face to face. Yeats writes in the simple, symbolic style of his early theatre, where an hourglass can measure a lifetime and a fool can speak wisdom.
7501-tales-of-the-wilderness:
Boris Pilniak, born Boris Vogau, was one of the first new voices of Soviet literature, and these stories show Russian fiction after Chekhov. Prince D. S. Mirsky introduces the volume, and F. O'Dempsey translated it into English. The tales carry titles like The Snow, A Year of Their Lives, A Thousand Years, Over the Ravine, and The Forest Manor.

Mirsky's introduction argues that the new literature reversed the Victorian balance, putting poetry and manner above prose and matter. Pilniak's wilderness tales live in that new manner: villages, forests, snow, and estates like the Bielokonsky estate, seen through a prose that is lyrical and unsettled. The book is a good first meeting with a writer the English public, as Mirsky says, knew next to nothing about.
7555-quotes-and-images-from-the-confessi:
Jean-Jacques Rousseau's Confessions, the founding autobiography of the modern self, is gathered here in quotations and images. A feeling heart the foundation of all my misfortunes, Rousseau says. The entries that follow show that heart at work. There is ardor for learning become so far a madness, aversion to singularity, and an author who must be independent of success.

All animals are distrustful of man, and with reason. All your evils proceed from yourselves. A man on being questioned is immediately on his guard, and adopted the jargon of books rather than the knowledge they contained. Being beat like a slave, Rousseau judged he had a right to resist. The collection gives Rousseau's restless, confessing voice in its most quotable sentences.
791-the-princess:
Alfred Lord Tennyson wrote this long poem about a prince who, with friends disguised as women, enters a college founded by Princess Ida for the education of women alone. The prologue sets the scene at a summer fete, where the tale is told in turn by guests. Love, debate, and war of the sexes follow, in blank verse of great beauty.

Tennyson weighs the claims of women's learning against the customs of his day, and he lets both sides speak with wit and feeling. The poem ends in reconciliation, not triumph for either side. It remains a landmark Victorian meditation on gender and education, and a showcase for Tennyson's musical line.
8-abraham-lincoln-s-second-inaugural-add:
Four years into civil war, Abraham Lincoln took the oath a second time in March 1865. His second inaugural address is short, sober, and free of triumph. He notes both sides prayed to the same God and read the same Bible.

Lincoln refuses to claim full blame or full credit for any side. He reads the war as a judgment on slavery, to be borne until its cause is removed. The closing plea asks for malice toward none and charity for all. It sets healing, not vengeance, as the work of peace.
8445-look-back-on-happiness:
Knut Hamsun's Look Back on Happiness, translated from Norwegian by Paula Wiking, opens with a man going to the forest. Not because he is offended or very unhappy about men's evil ways, he says, but because the forest will not come to him, so he must go to it. He goes this time not as a slave and vagabond, but with money enough, a changed man looking back.

Hamsun, later a Nobel winner, writes here in the reflective, solitary vein that runs through his work. The book's forest walk becomes a meditation on happiness, freedom, and the past. Readers of Hamsun will find the voice familiar: plain, proud, and close to nature, with happiness examined rather than chased.
866-the-cost-of-kindness:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote this comic story on the price of kindness, opening with little Mrs. Pennycoop's claim that kindness costs nothing. Her husband, an auctioneer of twenty years, retorts that it is valued precisely at cost price, for he has tested the public's taste for sentiment in his saleroom.

Jerome spins the exchange into a light tale of good deeds that go unthanked, and of the gap between fine words and real thanks. His humour is dry and domestic, with a sting in the tail. The story charms readers who know that kindness, though free to give, is rarely free to receive well.
9-abraham-lincoln-s-first-inaugural-addr:
Weeks before shots at Fort Sumter, Abraham Lincoln addressed a splitting nation in March 1861. His first inaugural address sought to calm Southern fears about slavery where it already existed. He disclaimed any lawful right or wish to interfere there.

Lincoln insists the Union cannot be broken by one side alone and pledges to hold federal property. He appeals to reason, the Constitution, and the bonds of affection between sections. The speech holds the door open to peace while warning that secession means war. Events soon closed that door. Its careful legal tone shows a president trying to hold a nation together without firing first.
99-collected-articles-of-frederick-dougl:
Frederick Douglass escaped slavery and became its most famous American critic. These collected articles open with My Escape from Slavery, written for The Century magazine in 1881. Douglass explains why he long withheld the details of his flight.

A second piece turns to Reconstruction and the unfinished work of freedom after the Civil War. Douglass writes with plain force about rights, voting, and the danger of forgetting. The articles show an elder statesman still arguing for justice. They belong beside his longer narratives of slavery and freedom. Douglass's voice in these pieces still speaks to debates over citizenship, memory, and equal rights.
9903-way-of-the-lawless:
Max Brand's western novel, first published in 1921 under the title Free Range, centers on Andrew Lanning, a young blacksmith's helper. Jasper Lanning, a seventy-year-old veteran who raised him, fears his life's work has failed, since Andrew seems made for trouble rather than the forge.

Andrew drifts toward the outlaw road, where loyalty, gun skill, and a hard code decide who lives. Brand writes lean, fast scenes of horses, workshops, and desert towns. The novel's pull is its hero's divided nature: a gentle hand at the anvil and a dangerous temper when pushed.
a-damsel-in-distress:
P. G. Wodehouse sets his romantic comedy at Belpher Castle in Hampshire, seat of the Earls of Marshmoreton since the fifteenth century, and refuses, with a wink, to spend pages describing it. The damsel is Lady Maud, kept at the castle by her family after a London attachment they dislike. The rescuer is George Bevan, an American composer of musical comedies.

Twenty-seven chapters tangle George's pursuit with a case of mistaken identity, a determined brother, a chorus girl, and the castle's pig-loving earl. Wodehouse times every entrance and misunderstanding like stage machinery. The tale is pure lightness, built from crisp dialogue, and it later reached the screen as a musical film.
a-dome-of-many-coloured-glass:
Amy Lowell published this, her first book of poems, in 1912, as the note in this printing records. The title comes from Shelley's Adonais: life, like a dome of many-coloured glass, stains the white radiance of eternity. Lowell's contents divide the book into lyrical poems, a run of sonnets, a long piece on the Boston Athenaeum, and verses for children.

The lyrics take up gardens, cities, art objects, seasons, and travel, often in the rich, image-heavy manner Lowell would soon push further as a leader of the Imagist movement. Sonnets on Keats, dreams, and dawn sit beside New York at night and a fairy tale in verse. The book shows a poet still partly traditional in form, already hungry for color and exact seeing.
a-great-success: Mary Humphry Ward tells of a great success through Arthur and Doris Meadows. The novel opens with a taxi fare dispute, half a crown paid where one and twopence was due. Doris runs to the window to call the driver back. Ward follows the couple through social life in a South Kensington house.
a-knight-of-the-white-cross:
A Knight of the White Cross is an 1895 historical novel by G A Henty. Young Gervaise Tresham leaves England and the turmoil of the Wars of the Roses behind him. He travels to join the Knights of St John, beginning as a page of the Grand Master, and he rises quickly to knighthood in the order.

As a knight, Gervaise defends Europe and Christendom against piracy in the Mediterranean and against the expansion of the Turkish empire. He is present at the defense of the fortress of Rhodes during its first great siege. Henty builds the boy's career into a tour of the Hospitallers' world, in his usual mix of schooling, battle, and honor.
a-man-of-business:
Honoré de Balzac begins with a word lesson: lorette, a slang term invented in 1840, he says, for a kept woman of Paris. Clara Bell and others translated the tale. From that sharp opening, the story moves into the world of Paris money, where reputations are bought and sold like goods.

At its center stands a man of business whose schemes run through debt, credit, and the debtors' prison. Balzac, who knew debt from his own life, draws the war between creditors and debtors with inside knowledge. Rogues, lawyers, and fashionable women cross the plot. The short novel reads as both entertainment and a guide to the cash heart of his Paris.
a-vindication-of-the-press: Daniel Defoe vindicates the press in this essay of 1718, reprinted by the Augustan Reprint Society with an introduction by Otho Clinton Williams. Published as number twenty-nine by the Clark Memorial Library in 1951, the tract argues the usefulness of the press at a time when its liberty was contested. Its survival in a modern scholarly reprint testifies to a classic early defence of printing against restraint.
abraham-lincoln-s-first-inaugural-addres:
Abraham Lincoln gave his first inaugural address on March 4, 1861, a date printed at the head of the text, with Southern states already leaving the Union. He speaks as a lawyer-president, aiming to calm fears. The South, he argues, has no cause to fear for its property, peace, or safety under his administration, and he repeats his pledge not to interfere with slavery where it already existed.

Much of the speech works through constitutional questions: the return of fugitives, the power of amendments, and why the Union cannot legally be broken. Lincoln insists he will hold federal property and enforce the laws, while avoiding bloodshed if the other side does not force it. The address ends as a plea to shared memory and the bonds of affection.
abraham-lincoln-s-second-inaugural-addre:
Abraham Lincoln delivered his second inaugural address on March 4, 1865, as the Civil War neared its end. The date is printed at the head of the speech. Lincoln speaks briefly, noting that the war's progress is known to all and that little new can be said. He names slavery plainly as the cause for which one side made war rather than let the nation survive.

Most of the address turns to God's purposes and to shared guilt for slavery across North and South. Lincoln asks that neither side judge the other, since both read the same Bible and prayed to the same God. He closes with the famous call for malice toward none and charity for all, urging the nation to bind up its wounds.
anna-the-adventuress:
Anna the Adventuress is a 1904 novel by E Phillips Oppenheim, built on a swap between two sisters. Annabel Pellissier, for reasons of her own, lets Sir John Ferringhall believe that she is her sister Anna. Anna allows the deception to stand, and so must carry her sister's reputation, which in Paris is that of a coquette.

When both sisters return to London, the mistaken identity breeds endless complications in love and society. Each sister is judged for the other's acts, and the truth becomes harder to confess the longer it is hidden. The result is one of Oppenheim's most intriguing stories of romance and imposture, driven by the double life at its center.
annajanska-the-bolshevik-empress:
George Bernard Shaw calls his short play frankly a bravura piece, written as a variety theatre turn for the Coliseum, with Lillah McCarthy in the lead and Charles Ricketts designing the dresses. He tells the story of its making in a long, funny preface. A twenty-minute sketch needed a dazzling figure, and Shaw supplied a grand duchess turned revolutionary.

Annajanska, a general's daughter, arrives among officers who cannot decide whether she is a prisoner, a princess, or the new power in the land. Shaw packs the tiny play with epigrams about revolution, rank, and sex. It is a trifle by design, made to show off a star, and it still sparkles.
aunt-jane-s-nieces-in-the-red-cross:
Edith Van Dyne, L. Frank Baum's series pen name, published this wartime volume in 1915 with Reilly and Britton of Chicago. The nieces fit out a hospital ship and sail toward the European war, with Doctor Gys deciding their course. Chapters move from the arrival of a boy and a girl to the firing line itself.

Little Maurie, the war's victims, and a coward's test fill the middle chapters. A surgeon tells Beth that one shattered soldier cannot recover: a shell tore a horrible hole, morphine alone keeps him comfortable, and he may talk if he wishes. Andrew Denton instead lies quiet, saving his thanks for her. Patsy defies authority, tardy justice arrives, and Baum's girls face industrial war without losing their series optimism.
britannica-1911-abbess:
Abbess receives an office entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. An abbess heads an abbey or convent of nuns, as an abbot heads monks, with like election, rights, and rule. Sisters choose her by secret vote from their own body, and a bishop's blessing with staff and cross installs her for life.

Trent set her age at forty, with eight years professed. She commands full obedience and can expel, under the bishop, yet cannot ordain, veil, or excommunicate, priestly acts barred to her. English abbesses signed at councils before presbyters in old days. Celtic houses joined monks and nuns under one abbess. German Stifte keep the title for noble ladies' homes to this day.
britannica-1911-abscess:
Abscess receives a medical entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, signed with the initials of Edmund Owen. An abscess, from Latin abscedere, to separate, is a collection of pus in body tissue, the fruit of bacterial inflammation. No septic germs, no abscess, the entry states flatly.

Lowered tissue vitality starts the train: congestion, effusion, a hard brawny mass softening at its centre. Skin thins, a slough forms and gives way, and pus escapes with pain relieved. Granulation tissue then fills the cavity, healing by second intention through scar. Treatment stands on evacuation and drainage, with scraping and antiseptic washing where needed. Spinal tuberculous collections get the same free drainage, placed low so nothing pools.
britannica-1911-abyss:
Abyss comes from a Greek word for bottomless, and the 1911 Britannica entry traces what different ages meant by a bottomless depth. Zoologists borrowed the adjective abyssal for the deep regions of the sea, with their own flora, fauna, and deposits. In heraldry, oddly, the abyss is simply the middle point of a shield.

Scripture gives the word its weight. In the Greek Old Testament it stands for the original chaos and for the Hebrew tehom, the surging water-deep under the earth that feeds springs and rivers. Later it becomes the place of the dead, and in Revelation a prison for evil spirits. Rabbinical and kabbalistic writers divided it into layered regions below the ocean bed.
britannica-1911-access:
Access, from the Latin accessus, means approach, or the means of approaching. The 1911 Britannica entry follows the word through several corners of law. In questions of legitimacy, a child's standing can be challenged. Proof that a husband had no access to his wife in the relevant period can show he was not the father.

Property law gives the word other work. Land beside a public road carries a right of access to that road. Land beside a navigable river carries the same right. Ancient windows bring a right of access to air and light. Parents, too, may claim access to children under the court's guardianship.
britannica-1911-albula-pass:
Albula Pass, a route through the Swiss Alps, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It had become the principal road from the north to the Upper Engadine in the canton of the Grisons. Travellers already used it in the thirteenth century. A carriage road crossing at 7,595 feet was built in 1865, yet for long the easier Julier Pass drew more traffic.

The opening of the Albula railway in 1903 vastly increased the pass's practical importance. The entry traces the route in detail: the Rhine valley from Coire to Thusis, the grand Schyn gorge cut by the Albula torrent, then Tiefenkastell, Filisur, and Bergun. Below the pass a great tunnel runs for over three miles. The descent through the Bevers glen reaches the Upper Engadine about five miles below St Moritz, fifty-six miles from Coire in all.
britannica-1911-aldine-press:
The Aldine Press, a famed printing house of Venice, put the classics of Greece and Rome into neat, sound books that men could carry. Aldus Manutius set the press up late in the fifteenth century. From its benches came the prized Aldine printings of the Greek and Latin masters of that age. For the founder's own tale, the notice sends readers to the piece on Manutius.

One gift to print outshines the rest: italics, the sloped type now used for stress and for titles the world over, first came from this house. Print history, the art and craft of type, is where the Aldine fame chiefly rests, and that one stroke of new lettering would earn the press its place by itself. Brief as the notice is, it marks a turn in how books look.
britannica-1911-barrow-in-furness:
Barrow-in-Furness, a seaport and borough in Lancashire, England, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as a town of remarkably fast modern growth. It stands on the Furness peninsula between the Duddon estuary and Morecambe Bay, facing the long low island of Walney across a narrow channel. Its population rose from only 325 in 1847 to 57,586 in 1901, a change the entry ties directly to iron.

Pure haematite iron ore in the Furness district started the rise. Barrow first exported ore to South Wales and the Midlands, then gained a railway in 1846, ironworks in 1859, and a large Bessemer steel company in 1866. Shipbuilding later passed steel in importance, with Vickers building warships there. Docks cut between Barrow Island and the mainland, a graving dock, paper-pulp, jute, and engineering works complete the picture.
britannica-1911-bass:
Bass is a word pulled apart in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica into different words that happen to share a spelling. The first bass, the same word as base but spelt under Italian influence from basso, means deep or low. In music it names the lower part in a composition's harmony, the lowest male voice, or the lowest member of an instrument family. The bass-clarinet, anchoring the clarinet group from below, is the example given.

Other basses have nothing to do with music. Bass, or bast, pronounced differently, is the fibrous bark of the lime tree, used in gardening for tying up plants and for making mats and soft plaited baskets. From the same tree come basswood, the American lime, and white basswood, a related species. Finally, the entry notes, bass is also the name of a fish that closely resembles the perch.
britannica-1911-bolan-pass:
The Bolan Pass is a route through the hills on the Baluch frontier, linking Jacobabad and Sibi with Quetta. It always mattered in British campaigns in Afghanistan. After the treaty of Gandamak in 1879, at the close of the first phase of the Afghan War, Britain held the route directly.

The pass was picked for the first line of the Sind-Pishin railway from the plains to the plateau. Floods wrecked the first track, which followed the Bolan stream, and the line was moved to the Mashkaf valley, rejoining the Bolan at Mach. A longer line through the Harnai valley took ordinary traffic in the end. The Bolan loop was kept for emergencies, the entry explains.
britannica-1911-brenner-pass:
Brenner Pass is the lowest major pass across the Alps, at 4495 feet, and one of the most used in every age. Writers call it the great gate of Italy, the route by which most Teutonic tribes entered the land. Side passes feed into it, which adds to its weight as a through road.

Between 793 and 1402 emperors crossed it no fewer than 66 times, a mark of its place in travel and war. A carriage road went over it as early as 1772, and a railway followed in 1864-1867. By rail the climb from Innsbruck to the top is 25 miles, and the full run down through Brixen, Botzen and Trent to Verona comes to 174 and a half miles.
britannica-1911-brown-bess:
Brown Bess was the British army's name for the flintlock musket its infantry once carried. The term covers the weapon of the 18th and early 19th centuries generally, and it fell out of use when the rifle replaced the smoothbore musket. The short entry is mostly a puzzle about the name itself, testing two explanations.

Brown is the easier half: it comes from the colour of the wooden stock, since the name is found well before the practice of browning musket barrels began. Bess is harder. It may be a joking female counterpart to the brown bill, the old weapon of British foot soldiers, or a corruption of buss, meaning box, as in blunderbuss. Either way the entry leaves the question open, with the stock's colour settled and the pet name debated.
britannica-1911-carcass:
Carcass is the dead body of an animal. As a butcher's term it has a narrower sense. It means the body without head, extremities and offal. This short 1911 Britannica entry sets out the word's uses. It also names a military device of the same name. A carcass was a hollow iron case filled with combustibles. Gunners fired it from a howitzer at targets. Its flames issued through holes pierced in its sides. It was meant to set fire to buildings and ships.

The word's origin is obscure, the entry says. Forms of it are common across the Romance languages. One guess joins the Latin caro, flesh, to a word for a chest. Another guess traces it to a Greek word for a quiver. The French carquois and Portuguese carcaz stand behind that guess. The whole notice is brief. It gives the two senses and the rival derivations.
britannica-1911-carrickmacross:
Carrickmacross is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a market town of County Monaghan, Ireland, 68 miles north-west of Dublin on a branch of the Great Northern railway. Its urban district held 1874 people in 1901. The town sits on a pleasant, raised site and carries on a fair trade in farm goods. Its best-known product is lace, made in several convent establishments.

Old remains give the short entry its history. Some ruins of an Elizabethan castle survive; it was a seat of the earls of Essex and was destroyed in the wars of 1641. The ruins of the old church of St Finbar mark the same hard period. Between the lace trade, the farm market, and these broken buildings, the entry offers a compact picture of a small Irish town and the troubles written into its stones.
britannica-1911-congress:
Congress, in diplomacy, is a solemn assembly of sovereigns or their full agents. Such a body meets to settle great questions of shared concern for good. The word comes from Latin roots for coming together. In this political sense it came into use in the 1600s. A lone case shows in 1636, for a papal meeting at Cologne on the Thirty Years' War.

In 1647 the peace talks at Osnabrück and Münster bore the name. Some men called the word coarse and unfit, yet it stuck. The United States took the name for its law-making body in a plain line from that use. The Continental Congresses of 1774 and after were congresses of states. So was the Congress of the Confederation that ran to 1788. The entry then weighs how great powers have shaped such meets. Their hand has ruled most congresses that changed the map.
britannica-1911-cuirass:
A cuirass is the plate armour that covers the front of the wearer's body, its name drawn from a Latin word for leather, its first material. In a full suit the term covers breast and back plates together. The lighter corslet, strictly a breast-plate only, stands beside it. Bronze and iron cuirasses served the armies of the ancient world. In medieval war, plate body-defence became standard only in the 1300s.

Through that century the cuirass spread until chain-mail all but vanished from knightly figures. It was worn covered, resting on the hips so the wearer could act freely. The long entry follows its forms down the centuries. Use faded, yet mounted cuirassiers kept breast and back plates into modern armies. After Waterloo, old cuirasses from the Tower of London were fitted again for the Life Guards and Horse Guards. Parade corps still wear leather versions.
britannica-1911-culross:
Culross, said locally as Coo-rus, is a royal and police burgh of Fifeshire in Scotland, with only 348 people. It sits on a hillside sloping gently to the Forth, west of Dunfermline. Until 1890 it belonged to a detached part of Perthshire. Its calm, old-world look matches its great age. St Serf worked there as a missionary, founded a church and cemetery, and died and was buried in the town.

Kentigern, first bishop of Glasgow, was born at Culross and raised by St Serf as a son. A Cistercian abbey followed in 1217, and its choir now serves as the parish church. James VI made the town a royal burgh in 1588. The embalmed heart of Edward, Lord Bruce of Kinloss, killed in a duel in 1613, rests in the abbey church in a silver casket. Coal, salt, and linen trades have faded, and the town now draws holiday visitors.
britannica-1911-furness:
Furness is a district of Lancashire cut off from the county by Morecambe Bay, covering about 250 square miles. Its northern half lies in the Lake District and holds the Old Man of Coniston and Wetherlam, while the Leven and Crake drain Windermere and Coniston Lake. The peninsula between the Duddon and Morecambe Bay is rich in hematite iron ore, worked from early times. Barrow grew up in the 19th century as the port for this ore, and furnaces followed when the Bessemer process created demand for non-phosphoric ore.

Furness Abbey, founded in 1127 by monks of the order of Savigny, joined the Cistercian order in 1148 and became the largest Cistercian house in the kingdom. Its abbot ruled the lordship almost absolutely, and gifts made the house rich, with revenues of £750 to £800 a year at the Dissolution. The abbot surrendered the abbey to the king on the 7th of April 1537.
britannica-1911-glass:
Glass, in the 1911 Britannica, is a very long technical article on a hard, usually transparent substance. It defines glass as a material that passes from a fluid state at high heat to a solid one too fast for visible crystals to form. Many varieties exist, differing widely in composition and qualities.

The opening sets out what most glasses share. They pass through a viscous stage in cooling, and take colour from metallic oxides fused into the mix. They conduct heat and electricity poorly. When broken, they show a shell-like fracture. The article then gives recipes, such as English flint glass from sand, potash carbonate and red lead. Furnaces, including the Siemens continuous tank furnace, are described and figured. Annealing, the slow cooling that keeps glass from cracking, gets full treatment. Later parts cover the branches of manufacture and the kinds of glass made in each.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbess:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on abbess defines the female superior, in spiritual and temporal matters, of a convent of twelve nuns or more. With few exceptions her position matches an abbot's in his monastery, though the title began with Benedictine superiors and spread to other orders, notably the Poor Clares and certain colleges of canonesses.

Women's monastic communities arose early in the East and reached the West toward the close of the fourth century, flourishing in Gaul, where tradition credits St. Martin of Tours with many foundations. Cassian founded a famous convent at Marseilles early in the fifth century, and St. Caesarius later placed his sister Caesaria over a new house at Arles. The entry traces the office's powers, election and history across the orders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abyss:
Abyss, from Greek abyssos, is first and classically an adjective for deep, very deep. Elsewhere in the Bible, and once in Diogenes Laertius, it is a noun. Some thirty times in the Septuagint it renders the Hebrew tehom, with Assyrian tihamtu behind it, and once each it renders terms for sea-deep, deep flood, and spacious place.

Hence it carries five meanings: primeval waters, waters beneath the earth, upper seas and rivers, the abode of the dead or limbo, and the abode of evil spirits, or hell. Only the last two meanings occur in the New Testament. The short entry thus maps one word across classical use, Hebrew sources, and Christian scripture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexander-gos:
Alexander Goss was the second Bishop of Liverpool, born at Ormskirk in Lancashire in July 1814 and dead at St. Edward's College, Liverpool, in October 1872. He came on both sides from old Lancashire Catholic families, his father from the Gooses or Gosses and his mother from the Rutters. His uncle, the priest Henry Rutter, sent him to Ushaw College in 1827, where he later taught as a minor professor, and he was ordained a priest in July 1841.

Returning to England in March 1842, Goss served at St. Wilfrid's in Manchester, then became vice-president of the new St. Edward's College at Everton in October of that year. He was consecrated coadjutor bishop by Cardinal Wiseman in September 1853 and became Bishop of Liverpool on Dr. Brown's death in January 1856. A tall, blunt, plain-spoken man and a powerful preacher, he built many churches and schools and championed Catholic education.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andreas-rass:
Andreas Rass, Bishop of Strasburg, was born at Sigolsheim in upper Alsace in 1794 and died at Strasburg in 1887. After classical training at Schlettstadt and Nancy, he studied at Mainz under Liebermann and was ordained priest in 1816. In 1825 he became director of the Mainz seminary and professor of dogmatics, and in 1829 superior of the Strasburg seminary for priests.

Made coadjutor Bishop of Strasburg in 1840 and consecrated in 1841, he became bishop in 1842. As bishop he trained the clergy, extended religious societies, and defended Papal Infallibility at the Vatican Council. His 1874 Reichstag declaration, that the Treaty of Frankfort was recognized by the Catholics of Alsace and Lorraine, shattered his popularity at home. Before his episcopate he founded the Katholik at Mainz in 1821 with Nicholas Weis and promoted missions through the German Annalen der Verbreitung des Glaubens. His important work, Die Convertiten seit der Reformation, appeared in thirteen volumes from 1866 to 1880.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-buttress: A buttress is a pier or mass of masonry that juts past the face of a wall. It strengthens the wall at set points and balances the push of a roof or vault. When the projection stands inside the wall it is called a counterfort. A flying buttress is an arch with one end on a detached pier, carrying the thrust of the nave vault across the aisles or cloister.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canon-of-the-:
The Canon of the Mass is the Roman Missal's name for the chief part of the Mass. It comes after the Offertory and before Communion. It is the Consecration prayer of the Mass of the Faithful. The Catechumens' Mass holds lessons and collects. The name canon means a norm or rule. It also names Scripture's canon, council canons, saints' lists, and church clerks.

In the Byzantine Rite a kanon is nine odes in singing order. The word has at times named the canonical Hours. In the West it now names the Eucharistic prayer. Gregory I's letters use it. The Gelasian Sacramentary heads it Incipit Canon Actionis. That name has stuck to this part from the seventh century on. Walafrid Strabo held it is called Canon as the lawful, regular making of the Sacrament. Benedict XIV held it the firm rule for the New Testament sacrifice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canoness:
Canonesses are women living in community for the Church's work, a practice reaching back to the earliest times. Saint Augustine of Hippo drew up the first general rule for such women in 423. It was addressed to Felicitas, superior of the Hippo monastery, and to Rusticus, the priest in charge of the nuns. Toward the end of the eighth century the title canoness first appears, given to communities that professed a common life yet did not keep Augustine's rule in full.

These canonesses copied the chapters of canons regular lately shaped by Chrodegang of Metz. They took only two vows, chastity and obedience, and their superiors, called abbesses, often held princely rank and feudal jurisdiction. Their work was the Divine Office, care of vestments, and schooling the young, above all noblemen's daughters. Some houses of secular canonesses still stand, Catholic and Protestant, several holding large properties.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caspar-henry-:
Caspar Henry Borgess was the third Bishop of Detroit, born at Kloppenburg, Hanover, in August 1824, who died at Kalamazoo, Michigan, in May 1890. He came to America as a boy, studied at St. Xavier's College in Cincinnati and St. Charles's Seminary in Philadelphia, and was ordained at Cincinnati in December 1847. After ten years at Columbus, he became rector of St. Peter's Cathedral, Cincinnati, in 1859.

Made administrator of Detroit and titular Bishop of Calydon in April 1870, he took the Detroit title only in 1871. The first bishop, Frederick Rese, never resigned despite long incapacity and died at Hildesheim that year. Borgess shifted the see from Belgian and French dominance toward the English-speaking regime the growing population needed. He brought in the Jesuits and resigned in April 1888 for retirement as titular of Phacusites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chapter-and-c:
A conventual Mass is the daily Mass said in churches where the Divine Office is said publicly every day. Joined with the canonical Hours, it forms the church's official daily public worship. In cathedrals and collegiate churches with a chapter it is often called the chapter Mass, though the official books use the general name conventual for it as well.

Churches of regulars bound to public recitation of the Office must also celebrate a daily conventual Mass, not a chapter Mass. This certainly covers monastic and canon-regular churches. Whether mendicant friars bear this obligation is disputed. Some authors hold them bound by common law, others only by their special constitutions or custom. Some extend the duty even to convents where nuns say the Office in choir. The duty of providing the conventual Mass falls on the corporate body and its superiors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Arthur Barry O'Neill's entry follows the Congregation of Holy Cross, priests and lay brothers under simple vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience, called Religious of Holy Cross. Its threefold purpose joins members' perfection through evangelical counsels, sanctification of others by preaching, especially in country places and foreign missions, and Christian education of youth. Born from reaction against Revolutionary hatred of religion and religious education, it took present shape when Rome united two French societies.

Dujarié gathered young men about 1820 as Brothers of Saint Joseph, primary teachers for parishes beyond the Christian Brothers' reach. Moreau founded the Auxiliary Priests of Le Mans in 1835, then became first superior general until 1866. Daily life joins meditation, Mass, examen, and beads. Algeria ranked among earliest missions. Bishop Bourget's 1841 requests seeded the Canadian province. The United States province, oldest and most extensive, grew from Notre Dame, Indiana, founded by Father Edward Sorin in 1842.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-consciousness:
Michael Maher's entry treats consciousness, Latin conscientia, German Bewusstsein, which cannot strictly be defined. Widely, it covers sensations, thoughts, feelings, and volitions, the sum of mental life. Contrast clarifies: conscious life against swoon or deep, dreamless sleep. We are conscious of mental states when alive to them or aware in any degree. Self-consciousness names the higher form, where we recognize states as our own. Modern times made consciousness the subject of psychology.

Ordered study is modern, though theology's problems long compelled close observation. From a Catholic view the main interest follows history's outline. Number science appears as psychophysics, seeking laws for intensity relations. Self-consciousness matters most in thought and psychology, showing mind at work. Odd forms vary the weight of self and states, while dreams and sleepwalking mediate normal and eccentric life. Daily consciousness, the discussion shows, stands shaped by hidden processes escaping notice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-covetousness:
A moral theology entry defines covetousness as wanting without reason what we do not own. In its broad sense it covers honours, fleshly pleasure, and riches. In its specific sense it looks to riches themselves, whether money or property, and to holding them rather than gaining them.

Numbered among the capital sins, it is called by St. Paul a root of all sins. Yet the entry is careful: the natural wish to acquire and hold possessions is not itself condemned. It becomes sinful when it defies justice or charity, makes wealth the end of happiness, or blocks duty to God and neighbour. Nursed into habit, it breeds perfidy, heartlessness, and unrest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daughters-of-:
A congregational entry traces the Daughters of the Cross, a French institute begun in 1625 at Roy in Picardy. Its founders were Father Pierre Guerin, Francoise Unalet, and Marie Fannier, and its aim was to give girls a Christian education. Its members at first took no vows, and civil misfortunes nearly wrecked the young society.

Later adherents met Marie l'Huillier de Villeneuve, who, encouraged by Saint Vincent de Paul, founded a house near Paris in 1651, introducing vows with Archbishop Gondi's approval. Older houses opposed the change, splitting the society into secular and religious branches, the latter winning papal approbation in 1668. Dispersed in the Revolution, the institute revived at Saint Quentin in 1828, was reorganized in 1837, and spread to Belgium and England.

A congregational entry presents the Daughters of the Holy Cross, also called the Sisters of Saint Andrew. Their aims were to instruct poor country girls, shelter the young exposed to temptation, prepare the sick for death, and care for churches. Sisters took yearly vows for five years, then perpetual vows, under diocesan control.

Founded at Guinnetiere near Bethines in the Diocese of Vienne in 1806, the congregation moved its motherhouse to Maille in 1811 and won approval of its constitutions in 1817. Government recognition came in 1819 and 1826, and the foundress bought the ancient abbey of La Puye in 1820 as headquarters. By the 1905 dispersion of French orders, the sisters held 400 houses in France, nine in Italy, and nine in Spain, with over 3,000 nuns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-joseph-:
Franz Joseph, Ritter von Buss, born at Zell in Baden on 23 March 1803 and dead at Freiburg im Breisgau on 31 January 1878, was a German jurist and Catholic social leader. He studied at Freiburg, taking doctorates in philosophy, law, and medicine, spent short stays at Bonn and Gottingen, passed a brilliant examination, and became city attorney. In 1836 he became ordinary professor at Freiburg, where his fearless treatment of vexed social and church problems won a large student following. He often lectured four or five times a day.

 Elected to Baden's Lower House in 1837, he addressed the social question and church rights. Despite failures he kept Catholics alert to current events, organising no fewer than four hundred Catholic associations and giving Baden's Catholics a sense of strength and resolve.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grey-nuns-of-:
Montreal's Grey Sisters sent four nuns to Bytown, now Ottawa, in February 1845 at a bishop's request. That Ottawa branch is the subject here. Sisters Elizabeth Bruyère and Helen Howard opened two classes at once, with more than 150 pupils, founding what became the Rideau Street boarding school. Another sister organized care for the sick poor.

Teaching and works of mercy run side by side through the entry. A hospital stood ready when Irish ship-fever victims arrived in 1847, and high schools, parish schools, children's homes, and a nurses' training school followed. Later houses stretch to Hull, Hudson Bay, Buffalo, Plattsburg, Ogdensburg, and Massachusetts, all under the Ottawa name Leo XIII fixed on them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-happiness:
Happiness, from good fortune in its first sense, became a central puzzle of Greek thought: what it is made of, what causes it, and how it differs from pleasure. The entry follows the question from Socrates and Plato, for whom happiness follows a soul in harmony, through Cyrenaics who gratified the senses and Stoics who suppressed them, to Aristotle's middle way.

For Aristotle happiness is not passive enjoyment but virtuous action, above all the contemplative life of the mind. It is enriched by friends and modest comfort over a full life, though only a few reach its highest form. Christian schoolmen took up his scheme, corrected by revelation. The entry sets his eudaimonia against modern hedonism's sum of pleasures and against Utilitarianism's felicities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-holiness:
Holiness, in New Testament language, joins two ideas: separation and sanction. The Vulgate word sanctitas renders two Greek words, hagiosyne and hosiotes. One points to separation, from a root meaning a matter of religious awe. The other points to what has received God's seal and approval. Confusion grew when the Reims version sometimes rendered a third word, hagiasmos, as holiness instead of sanctification.

St. Thomas insists on both aspects, separation and firmness. Sanctity marks all that is dedicated to divine service, whether persons or things. Such things must be pure and set apart from the world, so the mind can turn from lesser things to supreme truth. They must also hold firm, since holiness needs stability and not a passing mood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-baptis:
Johann Baptist Weiss, an Austrian historian born at Ettenheim in 1820 and died at Graz in 1899, studied modern languages and history at Freiburg, Tübingen, Heidelberg, and Munich. He taught French and English at Freiburg, lectured on history there in 1848 as a staunch Catholic party man, and edited the Freiburg Zeitung from 1850.

Quarrelling with Baden's government in 1852, Weiss took Graz's Austrian history chair, holding it from 1853 to 1891 and tutoring Archduke Charles Louis on travels to France and Constantinople. Ennobled in 1899, Weiss left a chief work. His thirty-two volume world history runs to the Congress of Vienna, dwelling above all on the eighteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-kaspar:
Johann Kaspar Zeuss, founder of Celtic philology, was born at Vogtendorf in 1806 and died there in 1856. Schooled at Bamberg gymnasium, he resisted parents' wish for priesthood, chose scholarship at Munich, and taught at its gymnasium after study, drawn to history and language.

Zeuss's 1837 book tracing Bavarians to Marcomanni won an Erlangen honorary doctorate. He taught history at Speyer to 1847, then at Munich university until poor health moved him to Bamberg lyceum. His monumental Celtic Grammar of 1853 made his fame. To reach Old Irish manuscripts he travelled to Karlsruhe, Würzburg, Saint Gall, Milan, London, and Oxford, copying sources and weighing modern dialects too.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-furniss:
John Furniss was an English Redemptorist who founded the children's mission and the children's Mass. Born near Sheffield in 1809 to a wealthy master cutler, he studied at Sedgley Park, Oscott, and Ushaw. He was ordained in 1834 and served at Doncaster until ill health sent him traveling eight years through Europe and the East as a pilgrim.

Returning in 1847, he worked among London waifs under the motto Suffer little children to come unto me. He joined the Redemptorists in 1851 and gave himself wholly to missions for children, lasting sometimes three weeks, for schoolchildren and working boys and girls alike. Holding that nothing disgusted children so much as monotony, he had prayers sung to simple airs. He kept sermons under twenty minutes, telling stories that moved audiences to tears. Over four million of his booklets sold across the English-speaking world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kinloss:
Kinloss is a Cistercian abbey on the Morayshire coast of Scotland, founded in 1150 or 1151 by King David I. Popular legend says a white dove led the lost king to safety while hunting nearby, and monks from Melrose settled the new house.

Pope Alexander III confirmed the foundation to Abbot Reinerius in 1174, and by 1229 Kinloss could send a colony to Culross. Rich gifts followed, including valuable salmon fishings on the Findhorn from Robert Bruce, confirmed by James I and James IV. Mitred abbots sat in Parliament. Edward I lodged there three weeks in 1303. Robert Reid, the most famed of its twenty-four abbots, treated with Henry VIII, built a library, and became Bishop of Orkney in 1541.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kiss:
The holy kiss was a farewell greeting ordered four times in St. Paul's letters, with St. Peter's version a kiss of love. Some scholars trace it to synagogue custom, though the evidence is thin. Early Christians seem to have used such greetings freely, even between men and women, as a sign of brotherly care.

Pre-Nicene fathers urged modesty about it, and Tertullian notes a pagan husband's dislike of his Christian wife greeting a brother with a kiss. The salute likely closed any gathering for Scripture reading and appears in some liturgies at the Mass of Catechumens. After baptism the new Christian was embraced by baptizer and congregation. A kiss also greets the newly ordained, the newly consecrated bishop, and, later, the crowned king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-knights-of-th:
The Knights of the Cross, in Latin Ordo Militaris Crucigerorum cum Rubea Stella, are a Bohemian religious order long used to bearing arms. That custom was confirmed in 1292 by an envoy of Pope Nicholas IV. The grand master still receives a sword at his induction, and popes and emperors have recognized the body as a military order.

Its roots are debated. Some trace it to Palestine fighters against the Saracens, others to a hospital brotherhood. No document shows Palestinian Cruciferi reaching Bohemia. It first appears as a fraternity serving a Prague hospital under Clarisses, founded by Princess Agnes in 1233. Richly endowed by the queen in 1235 and confirmed by Gregory IX, it became an order under St. Augustine's Rule in 1238. In 1239 it received the hospital in fief from the pope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liturgy-of-th:
The Liturgy of the Mass is a vast survey of the Latin Eucharist, its prayers and ceremonies from the earliest Church to modern times. Mass itself is a late Latin name, first loose in sense, that only slowly became the set term for the whole rite.

Earliest Rome spoke Greek, calling the rite Eucharistia, thanksgiving, a word Clement and Justin Martyr both use. Latin terms followed in the third century. The entry then walks through the rite part by part: its history, its shape, and its chants. It also tracks its shifts across centuries, with the sources that let scholars rebuild each stage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mary-howard-o:
Mary Howard of the Holy Cross was a Poor Clare, born 28 December 1653 and dead at Rouen in 1735. Daughter of Sir Robert Howard, younger son of Thomas, Earl of Berkshire, she spent early youth in his home. At eighteen, to escape Charles II's admiration, she went to Paris as Talbot and entered Val de Grace Benedictine convent to learn French.

Standing firm under persecution, she retired to Chaillot's Augustinian canonesses for several years, then joined Rouen's English Poor Clares as Parnel to guard her identity. She served successively as choir mistress, second and first portress, the latter managing the convent's temporal affairs. In 1702, on Mother Winefrid Clare Giffard's resignation after abbacy since 1670, she became abbess, governing with rare zeal and prudence till death. Her Chief Points of our Holy Ceremonies appeared in 1726, other works staying in manuscript.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-music-of-the-:
The Music of the Mass treats only those Mass texts that receive musical treatment. It leaves aside the Asperges, litanies and prophecies that cluster around the Mass in the Missal. Texts sung by celebrant and ministers in monotone with cadences are styled Accentus, while those assigned to the choir are Concentus. The Graduale Romanum supplies plainsong melodies for both.

Concentus divides into the Ordinary of the Mass, the Kyrie, Gloria, Credo, Sanctus, Benedictus and Agnus Dei, and the Proper, changing with feast and season. The Proper covers Introit, Gradual, Alleluia Verse, Sequence, Tract, Offertory and Communion. The entry traces how plainsong held its place, how polyphony and later styles treated these texts, and what rules govern their performance in the liturgy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nuptial-mass:
The Nuptial Mass, the Mass for bride and groom, stands last among votive Masses in the Missal and weaves marriage rite into Eucharist. Its lessons, chants, and prayers suit matrimony, and Tertullian already notes the oblation that confirms a marriage in the early third century.

Leonine, Gelasian, and Gregorian sacramentaries all carry the Mass, with a special Hanc Igitur and Preface, and Nicholas I's 866 instruction to the Bulgars describes crowning and communion of the couple. The entry follows later rubrics on blessings, communion, and second marriages. The Gelasian book adds a blessing now spoken after the Ite Missa Est and again after Communion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parochial-mas:
The parochial Mass serves a parish's people, above all for their welfare on Sundays and holidays of obligation, even if suppressed. The parish priest need not say it himself, but if he does not, he must have his own Mass said for that intention. Parishioners now meet their duty by attending Mass in any church.

Formerly they had to hear at least one Mass in the parish church, but that rule faded as religious orders won privileges. Trent treated it only as counsel, and despite later provincial rules it lapsed. The Mass need not be sung by common law, though statutes often require song, preceded on Sundays by blessing and sprinkling of water. Even unsung, it keeps added solemnity, with extra candles, two servers, instruction, announcements, and banns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pontifical-ma:
Pontifical Mass is the solemn Mass a bishop celebrates with the ceremonies laid down in the Ceremonial of Bishops. The full rite is used when he celebrates at the throne in his own cathedral, or by permission at the throne in another diocese. Canons vest in their order's dress, dignitaries in copes, priests in chasubles, deacons in dalmatics, and subdeacons in tunics.

Nine acolytes or clerics serve book, candle, mitre, crosier, censer, candles, gremiale, and cruets, with four more at the washing of the bishop's hands. The bishop also wears buskins and sandals, pectoral cross, tunic, dalmatic, gloves, pallium if entitled, mitre, ring, and gremiale, and a seventh candle burns besides the usual six. The entry follows his entry, vesting, and progress from throne to altar through the Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prioress:
A prioress, priorissa or praeposita, is a superioress in a women's monastic community. The title fits in strictness only a superioress in a convent with papal approbation whose members make solemn profession, that is, in convents of an order in the strict sense. In some places custom also gives the title to a superioress in a convent with only episcopal approbation, whose members make no solemn profession.

In general, a women's order gives its prioress the same office its prior holds for men. As first superior, the prioress rules her convent as a conventual prior rules his priory. Where an abbess stands first, the prioress's office matches a claustral prior's in an abbey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-processional-:
A processional cross is simply a crucifix borne at a procession's head, and, that it may be seen with ease, it is commonly set on a long staff or handle. It differs not in essence from the jurisdiction cross borne ere pope, legates, and metropolitans or archbishops. The pope may have the cross borne ere him wherever he stands. A legate's cross serves but in the land of his appointment, and an archbishop's but within his province. All these crosses, the pope's included, bear in practice but one bar.

The double barred cross counts as a sort of heraldic fiction, unknown in the Church's ceremonial. Cathedral chapters and like collegiate bodies commonly hold a processional cross that goes ere them in their corporate role, and the same holds for religious orders. For monastic orders usage bids the cross staff be silver or metal, but for mendicant orders, wood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prophecy-prop:
In the Old Testament, Yahweh barred Israel from all pagan oracles.  Yet He ever loathed divination and magic, augury and enchantment, and questioners of the dead. For the lack of other oracles, the Chosen People gained a gift unique in man's annals: prophecy.

The Hebrew prophet was more than a man lit by God to foretell events. Yahweh sent him as interpreter and supernaturally lit herald to speak His will to Israel. His charge was preaching as well as foretelling: to keep knowledge of the Old Law, to lead them back when they strayed, and to pave the way for the new covenant.  Three secrets of God demand deep respect, as they are most rarely revealed. They are conscience's state in this life, souls' state after death unless canonized, and predestination's mystery. Reprobation's secret was never revealed, since the soul in this life may still be saved.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reuss:
Reuss is the name of the two smallest states of the German Confederation, lying almost in Germany's centre, east of Thuringia on Saxony's western border.
