Together they cover 440 square miles: the elder line, Reuss-Greitz, 122 square miles with 70,603 people in 1905, and the younger line, Reuss-Schleiz, 318 square miles with 144,584. Slavonic races lived there in early medieval times, civilized and converted by Otto the First, and the region fell under Zeitz, founded in 968 as a suffragan of Magdeburg.

In religion the elder line counted 68,549 Lutherans, 1,205 Catholics, and 54 Jews in 1905, the younger 140,640 Lutherans, 2,806 Catholics, and 290 Jews. Catholics of the elder line passed under the Archbishop of Prague by a Brief of 15 March 1822, won through Princess Gasparina of Rohan-Rochefort, wife of Henry the Nineteenth. A Brief of 18 March 1874 placed them under the Vicar Apostolic of Saxony. The Greiz parish dates from 1897, its congregation's statutes winning government sanction that June with legal status.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ross:
Ross is a diocese in Ireland, founded by St Fachtna, whose place was known as Roscairbre and Rosailithir, Ross of the pilgrims. Fachtna founded the School of Ross and the see, dying about 590 on 14 August, his feast day. Bishops succeeded without break until after the Reformation. In 1207 King John granted Rosailithir to David Roche, ignoring the native chief O'Driscoll.

In 1306 the bishop's mensa was worth 26 marks, the cathedral 3 marks, and the tribal revenue only 45 pounds sterling. The diocese had 29 parishes in three divisions, a Cistercian abbey at Carrigilihy, and a Benedictine priory at St Mary's, Ross. From 1460 a Franciscan foundation stood on Sherkin Island from the O'Driscolls. Blessed Thady MacCarthy, appointed bishop in 1482, was deprived in 1488, translated to Cork and Cloyne in 1490, and died at Ivrea in 1492.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacrifice-of-:
The word Mass first became the general Western name for the Eucharistic Sacrifice after Gregory the Great. The early Church used breaking of bread or liturgy; the Greek Church has kept liturgy. Other early terms were the Lord's Supper, the Sacrifice, the gathering together, and the Mysteries. Love Feast, agape, did not necessarily carry the sacrifice idea.

Etymologically missa comes simply from missio, as oblata comes from oblatio and collecta from collectio. The reference was not to a Divine mission but simply to a dismissal, as echoed in Ite missa est. This solemn leave-taking was adopted from ordinary language. Bishop Avitus of Vienne wrote as late as 500 that Missa est is said when people are released from attendance. Popular speech then applied the dismissal ritual by synecdoche to the whole Eucharistic Sacrifice. The whole was named after the part.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-ros:
The School of Ross, now Ross-Carbery and once Ross-Ailithir, drew monks and students from across Europe to its halls. Its founder Fachtna, generally counted the same saint who founded Kilfenora diocese, since both feasts fall on 14 August and both trace him to the Corca Laighde princes, died young at forty-six. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a Munster teacher.

Born at Tulachteann, Fachtna learned piety first from Ita of Killeedy, the Brigid of Munster, then, some say, at Finnbar's seminary at Loch Eirce near Cork. He founded Molana monastery on Dririnis island in the Blackwater near Youghal. Home again, he raised a greater house on a rocky headland in his native land, and the entry traces Ross's fame as a school of saints and scholars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sign-of-the-c:
The sign of the cross covers manual acts, liturgical or devotional, that trace two lines crossing at right angles to figure Christ's cross. Most properly the term means the large cross drawn from forehead to breast and shoulder to shoulder. Catholics make it at the start of prayers, and the priest makes it at the foot of the altar. The entry describes the celebrant's hand in detail.

The same sign recurs through Mass and the Divine Office, and another kind is traced in the air in blessing. The entry traces the history of the gesture, from early finger symbolism for the Trinity, through Leo IV's ninth-century ruling on blessing, to the Western form familiar today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-maria:
Basile-Antoine Moreau founded the Sisters Marianites of Holy Cross in 1841 at Holy Cross parish near Le Mans in Sarthe, France. A priest of that city, he was born at Laigné-en-Belin on 11 February 1799 and dead at Le Mans on 20 January 1873. Moreau sent her with three other young women to the Good Shepherd superioress at Le Mans to prepare for religious life.

After a year's instruction he set them to help in the house founded at Holy Cross. They took the triple vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience on 4 August 1841. So formed the nucleus of a religious family, with Gascoin as first superior under the name Sister Mary of Seven Dolours from 15 September 1844. The rules won ten-year trial approval in 1867 and final approbation in 1885. The congregation counts two provinces, Louisiana with thirteen houses and France with ten, plus New York missions attached to France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-th:
Basil Moreau, professor of divinity at Le Mans, formed a society of auxiliary priests in 1834 after the French Revolution damaged religion and education. His bishop then made him superior of the Brothers of Saint Joseph, founded for school work in 1820. From these two groups grew the Association of the Holy Cross, which opened Holy Cross College in 1836. Young women offered help, and Moreau founded a sisterhood to teach girls.

The first candidates took the habit of the Congregation of the Seven Dolours from Moreau on 29 September 1841. After a year under Mother Dorothea they professed as Sisters of the Holy Cross. They were devoted to Our Lady of Sorrows and marked by a blue cincture and the chaplet of the Seven Dolours. Edward Sorin carried the work to Indiana, where Mother Angela Gillespie developed Saint Mary's of the Immaculate Conception at Notre Dame. Foundations spread to Canada and several American cities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-abban-of-n:
St. Abban of New Ross, also called Ewin, Abhan, or Evin, was the contemporary and namesake of St. Abban of Magheranoidhe, and this entry exists largely to undo a persistent confusion. His name has been locally corrupted into Stephen, Neville, and Nevin. And writers, Colgan and Lanigan among them, wrongly identified his foundation at Ros-mic-treoin, New Ross, with Rosglas, Monasterevan in County Kildare.

St. Evin of Rosglas, author of the Tripartite Life of St. Patrick, died on 22 December at his own house, Monaster Evin, while Abban, or Evin, of Ros-mic-treoin died at Ross in County Wexford. The entry is a short exercise in telling two saints apart, and a warning against trusting similar names.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-columba-of:
St. Columba of Terryglass was a son of Crinthainn and a disciple of St. Finnian of Clonard. This entry follows a man who, when Finnian was in extremis from the plague, administered Holy Viaticum to him. After finishing his studies, he took charge of Caemban, Fintan, and Mocumin, all counted among the saints.

In 548 he founded the celebrated monastery of Tirdaglas, or Terryglass. He is said to have visited Tours, bringing back relics of St. Martin. He died of the plague on 13 December 552 and was buried in his own Terryglass monastery's precincts. The Martyrology of Gorman mentions some fifteen other Irish saints bearing the name Columba.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-james-the-:
James the Less opens with a puzzle: the New Testament bears the name James for several men, and this entry sorts them. There is James son of Zebedee, apostle and brother of John, called Greater. There is James son of Alpheus, apostle. There is James, brother of the Lord. There is James son of Mary, brother of Joseph, called in Mark the little, not the less. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 weighs each claimant with care.

Its verdict, most highly probable and held certain by most Catholic interpreters, identifies the brother of the Lord with the James of Galatians, Acts, and Corinthians, bishop of Jerusalem's church. James brother of Jude follows, since Jude is called brother of James because James was better known. The entry is less a life than a piece of detective work, untangling names the Gospels reuse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-josep:
John Joseph of the Cross, Alcantarine Franciscan of Naples, fasted constantly, drank no wine, and slept three hours a night. Born on Ischia in 1654, he loved prayer and virtue from earliest years, and loved poverty so greatly he always wore the poor's dress, though nobly born. At sixteen he entered the Alcantarine reform at Naples, the first Italian to join that Spanish reform of Peter of Alcantara. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 5 March 1739.

In 1674 he was sent to found a friary at Afila in Piedmont, helping build it with his own hands. Much against his will he was raised to priesthood. As superior he insisted on performing the community's lowliest offices himself. In 1702 he became Vicar Provincial of the Italian Alcantarines. Gifted highly with miracles, he drew sick people of every condition, and his zeal for souls never flagged.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-of-th:
John of the Cross, co-founder of the Discalced Carmelites, wrote the Dark Night from a prison cell's consolations. Born at Hontoveros on 24 June 1542, youngest child of Gonzalo de Yepes and Catherine Alvarez, poor Toledo silk weavers, he knew hardship early. His father, disinherited for marrying below his rank, died young, and his widowed mother, helped by her eldest son, barely provided necessities. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death at Ubeda to 14 December 1591.

Schooled poorly at Medina del Campo and failed as an artisan's apprentice, he served seven years in Medina's hospital, waiting on the poorest while attending a Jesuit school. Seized on the night of 3 December 1577 by opponents of reform, he suffered over nine months' close imprisonment in a narrow, stifling Toledo cell. There heavenly consolations visited him, and after escape he wrote the Ascent and the Dark Night, incomplete works forming a full mystic theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-paul-of-th:
Paul of the Cross, founder of the Passionists, built an order around preaching Christ crucified. Born Paul Francis Danei at Ovada near Genoa on 3 January 1694, he learned from a priest schoolmaster at Cremolino and spent spare hours before the Blessed Sacrament. At fifteen he left school, refused an honourable marriage and a priest uncle's inheritance, keeping only the Breviary.

Vested in a black tunic by the bishop of Alessandria, he retired to a narrow cell to prepare his rule. His congregation, approved after long struggle, joined strict penance with popular missions on the Passion. He died at Rome on 18 October 1775, and his order spread from Italy across the world. The entry follows a mystic organiser from boyhood devotion to a worldwide institute.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stained-glass:
Stained glass, the popular name for coloured window glass, is strictly a misnomer, the entry insists. True stained glass is only one kind employed, produced by painting clear or coloured glass with silver oxide, which penetrates the glass under heat and gives a yellow reaction. Most coloured windows use pot-metal, glass coloured throughout while molten.

Pot-metal serves directly or toned, ornamented, or painted with vitrifiable pigments fused to its surface for figure subjects. Documentary and monumental history show glass in use from remotest ages, and the entry follows its craft from ancient windows through medieval cathedrals to modern revivals. It explains leading, painting, firing, and restoration in plain technical detail. Readers learn why usage fixed an erroneous name on a whole art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-league-of:
Drink, and the war against it among working Catholics, stands behind this short entry. Cardinal Manning founded the League of the Cross in London in 1873. This total abstinence confraternity joined clergy and laity to fight intemperance and lift religious, social, and domestic life, above all among the working classes.

London and Liverpool formed the chief centres, with branches across Great Britain, Ireland, and Australia. Rules demanded a pledge of total abstinence without time limit, Catholic membership alone, good practical Catholic life, and office-holding only for those who practised their faith. Papal indulgences and a yearly August conference sustained the league.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-true-cros:
Wood of Christ's cross, venerated across Christendom, is the relic at the centre of this entry, treated under cult, doctrine, relics, and feasts. Paul's letters already glory in the cross. He preaches rather than baptises, lest the cross be emptied. He writes of being nailed with Christ and reconciled by the cross, warned against its enemies, and boasting in nothing save the cross of the Lord. 

Growth of cult followed naturally, from early reverence to Helena's finding, divisions of relics, and feasts of Invention and Exaltation. Doctrine distinguishes veneration due to the cross from worship due to God alone. Principal relics, their journeys, and their critics receive balanced treatment in a long and learned survey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-veit-stoss:
Veit Stoss was a sculptor born at Nuremberg in 1438, who died there in 1533. In 1477 he set up a large workshop at Cracow in Poland, but in 1496 he came back to Nuremberg. With Adam Kraft and Peter Vischer, he ranks as the most important voice of late Gothic sculpture in Germany. A quick, skilled workman of great technical power, he pushed naturalism to extremes in youth, often at the cost of spirituality.

That edge may reflect his own character, since records of the age call him a restless, unquiet citizen. A certain lack of repose shows above all in his drapery, while his figures break free of Gothic convention and follow his own manner throughout. His later works show a deeper calm, the entry notes, and it lists his great altarpieces and tombs, above all the Cracow altar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-votive-mass:
A votive Mass is a Mass offered for a votum, a special intention, rather than for the day's appointed office. Normally Mass and Office form one whole, each day having its canonical hours and a corresponding Mass with the same collect and gospel, except on Good Friday. A votive Mass deliberately breaks that correspondence for a particular purpose.

The principle predates the name: almost from the Western liturgies' origin, with their calendar variation, Mass was occasionally offered with special prayers and lessons for a given intention. Augustine records a private Mass in Hesperius's house for his cure from an evil spirit. The earliest sacramentaries abound in votive Masses, the Leonine book offering Masses for bishops' anniversaries, drought, and against attackers, among many others for special needs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-way-of-the-cr:
The Way of the Cross, also called Stations of the Cross, Via Crucis, or Via Dolorosa. Names both a series of pictures or tableaux of scenes from Christ's Passion, each matching a particular incident, and the devotion connected with them. Stations may be stone, wood, or metal, sculptured or carved, or merely paintings or engravings. Ranged usually around a church's walls, sometimes outdoors on roads to a church or shrine, or in monastery cloisters.

General use came only toward the seventeenth century's end, though stations now stand in almost every church. Their number once varied widely, but fourteen are now prescribed: condemnation, the cross laid on Christ, his first fall, meeting his mother. The entry argues our present series and prayers likely derive not from Jerusalem itself. Turkish rule made devotion harder than at Nuremberg or Louvain, but from European imitation Ways of the Cross.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-witness:
Witness, in canon law, means one who testifies and furnishes proof in church affairs as in civil courts. A witness may be an eyewitness who saw an act, a signer attesting a document's execution, or a person examined under oath before a court or official. Catholic espousals under Ne Temere bind only when written and signed by both parties and two witnesses, or by a pastor or ordinary alone.

Lawful wedlock likewise needs a priest plus two witnesses, whom the Church wishes to be Catholics, though they sign no church paper. Sponsors at baptism and confirmation are not witnesses in this sense. Canonical precepts need the vicar general or two others present, and church papers are attested by chancellor or clerk. A witness must know the fact and speak truth; hearsay counts only when needed outside criminal matters, while the bribed, infamous, perjured, excommunicated, biased, or interested are barred.
chekhov-tales-garnett-1916-schoolmistres:
Constance Garnett published The Schoolmistress and Other Stories in 1916, a second volume of her Chekhov translations from that year. Garnett translated Russian literature on a vast scale, and her Chekhov volumes set the English text for decades. The schoolmistress of the title teaches in a Russian village.

Mary Vasilyevna, in Chekhov's story, rides to town for her small pay and dreams of a different life, then returns to her round of duties. Other tales in the volume turn on love, boredom, and small hopes in provincial towns. Chekhov's sympathy covers even his weakest figures. Garnett's volume deepened the English discovery of a writer now counted among the masters of the short story.
collected-articles-of-frederick-douglass:
Frederick Douglass wrote the pieces gathered here late in his life, and the hosted text holds the two essays named in its contents. The first, My Escape from Slavery, appeared in a national magazine in November 1881. Douglass had kept the manner of his escape secret for decades, to protect those who helped him and those who might follow. With slavery dead, he finally tells the story plainly.

The second piece, Reconstruction, looks back at the years after the Civil War, when the country tried to rebuild the South and secure the rights of the freed people. Douglass, who had met presidents and pressed Lincoln hard, writes as witness and judge. Together the essays show his clear, forceful prose at its ripest.

dr-heidenhoff-s-process:
Edward Bellamy's Dr. Heidenhoff's Process opens in the conference room of a Newville prayer meeting, where the clock points to ten minutes to nine. Deacons, brothers and sisters take their usual parts, while the meeting's hearers listen in strict, familiar order.

From that small-town religious world the story turns to guilt and memory, and to a doctor who claims a process for blotting out the remembrance of wrongdoing. Bellamy asks whether a conscience can be eased by science, and what a man loses when his past is taken from him. Readers who know Bellamy from Looking Backward will find here a shorter, darker tale of moral invention.
five-thousand-an-hour-how-johnny-gamble-:
George Randolph Chester built Five Thousand an Hour as a fast comic romance about money made at a gallop. Johnny Gamble, a charming promoter down to his last hundred dollars, loses at the racetrack as the story opens. He owes his missing partner's debts through a defunct irrigation company. Then he catches sight of Constance, a beautiful heiress, in the grandstand boxes.

Johnny resolves to win both the lady and a fortune by sheer speed of dealing. Chapters follow him through rapid business deals, a dreamed twenty-story hotel, and a fair where he trades between the babies' charity stalls. Rivals and old aristocrats block his path, and spot cash is demanded more than once. Chester keeps the pace breathless, letting Gamble's nerve, humour, and honesty carry a tale about American hustle and love.
fruitfulness:
Zola made this novel a plea for large families in a shrinking France. Its hero, Mathieu Froment, builds a fruitful farm at Chantebled. His growing household stands for life and work. Around him, Paris households limit their children and decay. The Seguin home, rich and divided, shows the contrast. A governess and a wrecked marriage mark its decline.

The book opens a planned series of four novels. Work, Truth, and Justice were to follow Fruitfulness. Ernest Vizetelly translated and edited this English version. His preface explains Zola's design at length. The story mixes farm scenes with drawing-room drama. Zola argues through lives rather than lectures. Children, land, and labor carry his gospel.
further-foolishness:
Leacock's Further Foolishness collects sketches and satires on the follies of the day. Stephen Leacock published it in 1916, from McGill University in Montreal. The contents group the pieces under heads: Follies in Fiction, Movies and Motors, Peace, War, and Politics, and Timid Thoughts on Timely Topics. Early pieces mock fiction itself, with fifty stories crushed into one and a Russian novel rendered with a hand pump. Movie and motor pieces follow.

The war pieces treat Germany, Mexico, and the peacemakers with dry scorn. A White House sketch views power from outside. The closing pieces ask whether the rich are happy and what humor is. The tone stays light over sharp points.
gettysburg-address:
Abraham Lincoln spoke at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, on November 19, 1863, at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery. The Civil War was still being fought, and thousands of soldiers killed in the battle there had been buried in its ground. Lincoln, as president, was asked to give a few formal remarks.

In roughly 270 words he recalled a nation founded on the claim that all men are created equal, then framed the war as a test of whether such a nation could endure. He honored the dead, said the living could not truly consecrate the ground, and urged them to finish the work the soldiers had begun.
govdocs-archive_org-996DunblaneMassacreS: An alternate capture of a tag archive headed Lord Cullen preserves material tied to the Dunblane massacre inquiry. Lord Cullen chaired the public inquiry into the 1996 Dunblane school shooting in Scotland, and his report shaped British gun law. A capture of this kind keeps web material as it was found, not as an edited text. Beyond its subject and form, the record gives little detail of contents. It is held for researchers of the case.
govdocs-archive_org-lucian-the-syrian-go:
Lucian of Samosata, the second-century Greek satirist, wrote The Syrian Goddess as an account of the goddess Atargatis and her great temple at Hierapolis in Syria. The work reads as travel writing, though from Lucian readers always suspect a raised eyebrow.

He describes the temple, its priests, its festivals, and its strange rites in detail, along with the miracles claimed for the goddess. Notes on the coins of Hierapolis accompany the text in this edition. The result is both a real source on an ancient cult and a performance by antiquity's sharpest wit, and scholars still argue over where one ends.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MerklePress_Mer:
Harold Weisberg wrote this letter on November 11, 1966, in a fight over printing his book 'Whitewash.' The book was his attack on the Warren Report, published at his own expense. Weisberg objected that his publisher had written contract terms into the printing agreement that the two men had never agreed upon.

Self-published critics depended on small printers and distributors, and disputes like this one could kill a book. Weisberg's letter states his objections in his usual direct style. It shows the unglamorous business underneath the assassination debate: contracts, print runs, and money. The first 'Whitewash' reached readers anyway, and letters like this record what that cost its author in time and temper.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PaladinPress_Pa:
Paladin Press advertised a manual by Raymond M. Momboisse titled 'Confrontations, Riots, Urban Warfare.' The book teaches tactics against civil disorder and urban guerrilla warfare. Paladin Press built its catalog on such titles: military and police technique sold to the public by mail.

The advertisement belongs to the years after the riots of the 1960s, when officials and citizens alike studied crowd control as a craft. Momboisse was a legal official who wrote on riot duty for professionals. An ad for his manual, clipped and filed, shows the literature of order that circulated beside the literature of protest. It also marks the readership Paladin served: men preparing, in print, for the next disturbance.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-USSRInformation: Harold Weisberg wrote to the information officer at the USSR Embassy in Washington on July 2, 1991. The Soviet Union had only months left to exist when the letter was sent. Weisberg, the veteran assassination researcher, kept up a wide correspondence with officials at home and abroad. The letter shows him still working his contacts and questions in the last summer of the Cold War.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WestJeanMiss_We: Miss Jean West is named in the title of this declassified US government document from the Internet Archive. The catalog supplies no date, office, or gist. The text has not surfaced in public. A woman's name kept in the files.
heart-of-darkness:
Joseph Conrad wrote Heart of Darkness, published as a serial in 1899 and in book form in 1902, and it became his most famous work. On a yacht in the Thames, the sailor Marlow tells of his trip up the Congo River as captain of a steamboat for a trading company. He is sent to fetch Kurtz, a brilliant ivory agent at a far station, spoken of with awe by everyone on the river.

The trip strips away, station by station, the fine words about trade and progress, showing theft, cruelty, and rot. Kurtz, found dying, has made himself a god among the local people and filled his post with horror. Marlow's last interview and his lie to Kurtz's fiancee close the tale. The novella's charge against empire still burns.
i-n-r-i-a-prisoner-s-story-of-the-cross:
Peter Rosegger wrote this prisoner's story of the Cross, translated by Elizabeth Lee. The London first edition came in September 1905, and two more followed by December. A prologue crowds a city square before the law courts. Electric cars halt while the crowd waits for a verdict to be cried.

The prisoner at the tale's heart retells the story of Jesus. A publican with a bad name longs to see the Prophet face to face. He dares not go, yet Jesus comes to those who wait humbly, the text says. Rosegger, an Austrian peasant's son, writes faith in a plain, warm voice. The frame makes the Gospel a condemned man's comfort.
in-the-wilderness:
Robert Hichens published In the Wilderness in 1917, a long novel in four books. The books are named Hermes and the Child, Echo, Little Cloisters, and The Unknown God. It opens in Milan in autumn 1894, at the Hotel Cavour. Amedeo Dorini, the hall porter, studies travelers as the omnibus returns.

Rosamund's party laughs under the eaves of an old house in a later scene. A gate in an ancient archway shuts them into their great garden with joy. Love, faith, and loss move the cast between England and the East. Hichens writes a slow, rich tale of the spirit.
inaugural-presidential-address:
Bill Clinton gave this inaugural address at noon on January 20, 1993, as the note at its head records. The transcript marks emphasis and pauses in his delivery. Clinton says America celebrates the mystery of renewal in the depth of winter. By words and faces, he says, the nation forces the spring.

He salutes President Bush for half a century of service. He calls each generation to define what it means to be an American. Responsibility from all, not something for nothing, is his demand. The speech is short, and this note describes only its own text and occasion.
jess:
Jess, by H Rider Haggard and first published in 1887, is a South African novel of two sisters and a villain in the years around the first Boer war. Haggard's contents bring the sisters to Mooifontein, a farm, and introduce Mr Frank Muller, who asks Bessie in marriage while Jess, the elder and stronger sister, watches. John, the Englishman who loves and is loved where he should not be, has adventures and escapes of his own.

The storm breaks, Jess goes to Pretoria, and Jantje tells his story. Chapters move through passes, drifts of the Vaal river, and the twelfth of February, toward a condemnation to death and a parting Jess herself demands. Muller shows his hand, Tanta Coetzee rides to the rescue, and vengeance closes the account. Haggard writes the Transvaal from inside settler fear and loyalty, with Jess as one of his fiercest heroines.
john-f-kennedy-s-inaugural-address:
John F. Kennedy's inaugural address, given on January 20, 1961, is the speech of a new president taking office. Kennedy calls the day not a victory of party but a celebration of freedom. He notes that humans now hold power to end all poverty and all life itself. Yet the old belief stands: rights come from God, not from the state.

The speech pledges that America will pay any price and bear any burden for liberty's survival. To old allies it promises loyal friendship, and to new states, no swap of colonial rule for iron tyranny. To the poor of the world it offers help to help themselves. Its summons to service made it one of the most remembered speeches of its century.
leaves-of-grass:
Walt Whitman built Leaves of Grass as the book of his whole life. It opens with a call from his soul to write verses for the body. Body and soul, he insists, are one.

The first book, Inscriptions, begins with One's-Self I Sing. Whitman sings a simple, separate person, yet speaks for all. Grass, earth, trees, and waves fill his rolling lines. He kept expanding this collection across many editions. It remains America's boldest experiment in free, democratic poetry. Whitman published the first edition himself in 1855. Song of Myself, his longest poem, anchors the growing book.
little-rivers-a-book-of-essays-in-profit:
Henry Van Dyke praises profitable idleness in these essays. He dedicates the book to his little daughter Brooke. Her heart, he writes, is like a mountain spring. Her thoughts sing like merry rivers beside him.

Contents wander from little rivers to a leaf of spearmint. Ampersand and the Ristigouche bring readers to fishing waters. Alpenrosen, goat's-milk, and trout-fishing in the Traun cross the Atlantic. Van Dyke preaches leisure spent outdoors with books and streams. A handful of heather and Au Large widen the fishing map. At the sign of the balsam bough closes the contents.
lizzy-glenn-or-the-trials-of-a-seamstres:
T. S. Arthur published this seamstress's tale in Philadelphia in 1859. Hood's Song of the Shirt supplies the opening epigraph. Work, work, work, till the brain begins to swim, it moans. Lizzy Glenn first appears beside Mrs. Gaston and her sick child.

Chapters ask how a needlewoman actually lives. A stranger takes interest in Lizzy after the child's death. Perkins's narrative later reveals a long-lost Eugenia. Arthur turns a seamstress's wages into social protest fiction. The father's dream and penny-saved tales follow Lizzy's story. Perkins anxiously seeks Lizzy before finding his lost Eugenia.
look-back-on-happiness:
Knut Hamsun's narrator withdraws to the forest in this book. Paula Wiking translated it from the Norwegian. He insists no offense or unhappiness drove him out. The forest would not come to him, so he went to it.

He arrives overfed and stupefied with success and good fortune. Like a sultan, he exchanges rich food for a hair shirt. Snowflakes, birds, and beasts keep his solitude eventful. He seeks the woods to roam, think, and heat great irons. Nietzsche would have spoken thus, the narrator imagines ironically. He simply went to the forest, he insists at last.
mary-minds-her-business:
George Weston published Mary Minds Her Business in 1920. He starts with a preface on his heroine's forebears. The line goes back to Josiah Spencer, a blacksmith in the late 1600s.

Josiah wed Mary McMillan, bought land by the Quinebaug River, and built a shop. A mill wheel, a grist mill, and a saw mill followed. His son took the sign Josiah Spencer and Son in time. Weston's Mary inherits that long line of work and grit. Twelve children came to the young Josiah's home in time. The Spencer line grows with the mills and the town round them.
mastery-of-self-for-wealth-power-success: Frank Channing Haddock wrote Mastery of Self, and the full title adds For Wealth, Power, Success. Project Gutenberg lists the text as its number 4286, first posted in 2001. The hosted sample for this entry preserves only the file header and license notes. No readable page of the book itself appears in the sample. This note stays with the title, the author, and the source for that reason.
metlakahtla-and-the-north-pacific-missio:
Eugene Stock tells the story of the Church Missionary Society's North Pacific mission. Its center was Metlakahtla, a Christian Indigenous village on the British Columbia coast. Three chapters reprint an 1868 pamphlet on ten years' work among the Tsimshean Indians. The rest draws on the Society's own periodicals and reports.

The book follows the call, the missionary William Duncan, and the first years of work. It describes the field, the people, and the settlement's growth. Stock writes as an advocate for the mission and its methods. Modern readers will also see the era's colonial assumptions at work in its pages.
nasa-tm-19660018729-current-status-of-pl:
William F Brown Jr and John E Srawley at Lewis Research Center reviewed the state of crack toughness testing in a paper for a June 1966 materials meeting in Atlantic City. Their subject is how well a material resists a crack that wants to run. Tests use specimens cut with a sharp notch, then loaded until the crack extends. Plane strain conditions, the strictest case, frame the work.

A toughness value lets a designer judge whether a flaw is safe or fatal. Without it, thick parts must be trusted on hope alone. Brown and Srawley survey how the testing stood at the time. Their field, fracture mechanics, was then becoming a standard part of aircraft and rocket design.
nasa-tm-19690006039-empirical-characteri:
Marcus F. Heidmann of Lewis Research Center characterizes strong acoustic pressure waves in this report. The waves were measured at the wall of a short cylindrical cavity. Inside, a relatively pure traveling transverse acoustic mode was running at high amplitude.

At minute amplitudes, pressure varies in a simple sine pattern. Harmonic distortion grows with amplitude and changes the wave shape substantially. Heidmann evaluated the measured wave shapes for their harmonic content. A simple cosine series relation represented the shapes well. It worked even as peak-to-peak amplitudes approached the mean cavity pressure. The relation gives analysts a convenient way to describe strong wave shapes. Rocket combustion chambers are one place such strong acoustic modes matter.
nasa-tm-19700003065-twentieth-semiannual:
NASA's Twentieth Semiannual Report to Congress covers July 1 through December 31, 1968. The period includes NASA's tenth anniversary, since the agency began in 1958. It also includes space flight activities through the pioneering flight of Apollo 8.

The transmitted account surveys agency progress for the President and Congress. Editors G. B. DeGennaro, H. H. Milton, and W. E. Boardman of the Office of Public Affairs prepared the volume. A White House message dated November 13, 1969 forwards the report. That message credits a decade of broad earlier work for the later Moon landing. The report stands as NASA's official half-year record for late 1968.
nasa-tm-19720002627-aircraft-measurement:
T Wilheit and colleagues flew microwave sensors over Arctic sea ice for this NASA study, issued as NASA TM X-65742. Every surface glows faintly in microwaves, and ice and open water glow differently. The team measured that emission from an aircraft at eight wavelengths. Their goal was to map where sea ice ended and open water began. Such maps matter for shipping, weather work, and polar research.

The expected contrast between ice and water appeared at every wavelength. From those readings, the team mapped the spread of sea ice and open water. The work showed that an aircraft could chart ice cover from the air. It did so without waiting for clear skies or daylight. Later satellite ice mapping grew from methods like these.
our-nervous-friends-illustrating-the-mas: Robert S. Carroll, a physician of Asheville, North Carolina, wrote Our Nervous Friends in 1919. It is the case-book companion to his Mastery of Nervousness. The hosted sample shows the title page and chapter headings only. Each heading carries its lesson: friendly nerves, the neurotic, the price of nervousness. Wrecking a generation and the nervously damaged mother follow. No case narrative appears in the sample.
out-of-time-s-abyss:
Edgar Rice Burroughs sends Bradley out of Fort Dinosaur in Out of Time's Abyss, the third of his Caspak tales. On September 4, 1916, Bradley leaves the fort with four companions. Sinclair, Brady, James, and Tippet march with him. They will search the base of the barrier cliffs. A scalable place would mean escape from the lost world of Caprona.

The five march waist-deep in lush jungle grasses starred with gorgeous blooms. Meadows and forests of eucalyptus and giant ferns follow. Caspak's teeming life hunts them at every step. Their rifles seldom cool. A hideous growl from a thicket stops the column in the first pages. Burroughs's prehistoric island runs on such moments.
over-the-pass: Frederick Palmer's Over the Pass, published in 1912, is a western novel. Its hero is Jack, a rider in spurs. The hosted sample shows the title page and contents only. Part One, An Easy Traveller, promises Dinosaur or Desperado. Jack carrying the mail and Señor Don't Care follow. A journey on crutches and the desert in bloom close the part. No chapter text appears in the sample.
peregrine-s-progress: The hosted sample shows only the front matter of Peregrine's Progress, the title page and contents, with no chapter text visible. The record dates Jeffery Farnol's novel to 1922. The contents open with an Ante Scriptum and a first book called The Silent Places, in which Peregrine introduces himself, sets forth upon a quest. He meets an extraordinary tinker and a down-at-heels gentleman, and hears the woes of Galloping Jerry, a notorious highwayman.
podcast-dannyjones-EvT_UemLqss:
Matt Cox is a former con man turned true-crime storyteller. He joins Danny Jones with one of his strangest tales. It concerns a man presented as an MK-Ultra victim. In Cox's telling, the story means country star Garth Brooks is not who the public thinks he is. The episode plays the claim for both mystery and comedy.

Cox's gift is narration, and Jones lets him spin the whole yarn before picking at its threads. Nothing here should be taken as established fact about anyone; it is a storyteller's story about another man's claims, delivered as entertainment. The episode's place in the series is as a tall tale hour, and it knows it. Listeners get a fraudster-turned-raconteur at work on material where fraud, delusion, and government crime blur together, and sorting them is left as an exercise for the audience.
podcast-joerogan-A78LaTBt3Ss:
Biologist Bret Weinstein sits for episode 2101 of the Joe Rogan Experience, one of many visits in his run as a house contrarian. Weinstein, a former professor, built a large audience by challenging health and campus orthodoxies. Rogan gives his guests long leashes, and Weinstein uses his.

The talk ranges over the subjects Weinstein returns to: evolution as a lens on modern life, the failures he sees in experts, and the cost of dissent. Rogan probes where he can and lets the monologues run where he cannot. Listeners get Weinstein's worldview stated whole, by the man himself, at full length.
podcast-tuckercarlson-kut47PODRSs:
Qatar's prime minister speaks with Tucker Carlson about war risk, diplomacy, and his country's image. Qatar hosts talks and seeks to calm tension around Iran. The episode title notes attacks on him in Western media.

The talk opens with the World Cup and Western lectures on Qatari customs. The prime minister says critics used the games to attack his nation. From there the pair turn to talks aimed at stopping a wider war. Listeners hear how a small Gulf state presents its role as a go-between in a tense region.
podcast-tuckercarlson-zfI-JZEBNss:
Tucker Carlson gives his full speech at the memorial for Charlie Kirk, and this file holds that speech with clips of their best talks. The title names their shared ground: God, Christianity, and hope. Kirk was a young leader on the right.

Carlson honors his friend in a eulogy that turns on faith more than on fights. The clips recall their talks on God and the hope that held them. The mood is grief with a spine of belief. Listeners get the full speech in one place, as it was given. The library keeps it as a record of a public farewell.
polly-and-the-princess:
Emma C. Dowd wrote Polly and the Princess, published in 1917, continuing the story of the Polly she introduced in Polly of the Hospital Staff. Dowd lists her earlier books proudly: the hospital Polly, Polly of Lady Gay Cottage, and Doodles, whose name reappears in the chapter titles here. Polly has grown from a children's-ward favorite into a young woman whose cheer is now wanted by grown people. Including a princess in disguise among the guests of a home for convalescents.

Contents promise waffles and dewlaps at the breakfast table, Polly addressing a board of managers, a hiking club, hilltop days, and a martyr named Alice Twining. Romance threads through the comedy, with a David to be loved by the end and a Mrs. Tenney to visit. Dowd's Polly books sold kindness as adventure, and this sequel widens her stage.
princess:
M. G. McClelland wrote the novel that opens this record, issued in New York in the American Authors' Series with a copyright of 1886. General Percival Smith, a former brigadier, plans to move his family from the city to a farm in Virginia, and the plan sets the household in an uproar.

His daughters Norma and Blanche lead the protest, picturing cows, snakes, corn bread, and slow mails in place of city comforts. Their clash between town polish and country life drives the opening chapters. The story gives a lively picture of family argument and social pride in postwar America.
pulpit-and-press:
Mary Baker Eddy, founder of Christian Science, gathered her sermons and press notices in a book copyrighted in 1895 and later issued by the trustees under her will. She dedicates it to the children whose gifts built the Mother's Room of her Boston church.

Eddy records that twenty-six hundred children gave a total of four thousand four hundred sixty dollars for that room in the First Church of Christ, Scientist. The volume joins a dedicatory sermon and related pieces with clippings that show how newspapers received her work. Readers get Christian Science presented by its founder, in her own pulpit voice.
quotes-and-images-from-the-confessions-o:
Quotes and Images from the Confessions of Rousseau sets out short passages from Jean Jacques Rousseau's Confessions in alphabetical order, prepared by David Widger. Few books bare a life so frankly, and the extracts keep Rousseau's mix of pride, grievance, and self-knowledge.

A feeling heart, the first line says, was the foundation of all his misfortunes. A man on being questioned is immediately on his guard, all animals are distrustful of man and with reason, and an author must be independent of success. Beaten like a slave as a boy, he judged he had a right to all vices, a wound the Confessions return to often.
risen-from-the-ranks-or-harry-walton-s-s:
Horatio Alger, Jr., author of Ragged Dick, published this tale of Harry Walton's success in 1874. He inscribes the volume to Thomas E. Barry of the Boston bar. A preface explains that the book continues Harry's history from Bound to Rise, and gives a summary of his earlier life in its first chapter.

Alger says he avoided the strange incidents and great strokes of luck that story writers command. He wanted a career that thousands of boys in Harry's place could imitate. The tale was suggested in part, he adds, by the career of an eminent American editor. Honest work, not chance, lifts his hero from the ranks.
saint-s-progress: John Galsworthy wrote a work headed Saints Progress, with no apostrophe in the heading shown here. The contents divide the book into parts made of numbered chapters with no titles given. Part I lists ten chapters, numbered I through X. Part II then starts again at I, and the listing shown here runs through VIII. No preface, cast, or opening passage appears in the portion shown here.
satow-jesuit-mission-press:
Ernest Satow published The Jesuit Mission Press in Japan in 1888. The diplomat-scholar catalogues a lost age of print in this study. Jesuits ran a press in Japan from 1591 to 1610, before expulsion.

The missionaries printed books in Japanese with roman letters for converts. Satow hunts down the rare survivors in libraries across the world. He lists each title, press, and copy with a scholar's care. The treasures of Japan's first age of print stand recorded here. His bibliography remains a landmark for book history in East Asia today. Satow turns a dry list into a tale of loss and rescue.
sienkiewicz-in-desert-and-wilderness:
Two children cross Africa in Sienkiewicz's adventure tale In Desert and Wilderness, here in English. Stas and Nel are seized in Sudan during the Mahdist rising. They break free and face desert, beasts, and sickness on the long road to safety.

Loyal African friends aid the pair at every turn of the road. Courage, quick wits, and kindness keep the children alive. Sienkiewicz fills the tale with rich detail on lands and peoples. Written for young readers, it has thrilled them in many languages for over a hundred years, and it shows its author's gift for swift, clear storytelling.
t-mann-royal-highness:
A minor German prince with a withered arm finds purpose, and love, in Thomas Mann's Royal Highness, read here in A. Cecil Curtis's English translation. Klaus Heinrich lives a life of pure ceremony in a tiny, fading principality. An American heiress and her father's millions arrive to disturb that gilded uselessness.

Lighter than Buddenbrooks, the novel keeps Mann's irony about art, duty, and modern money fully awake. The prince's formal existence slowly bends toward real work and real feeling. Mann called it a fairy tale, and its charm is genuine. Yet questions about what public roles do to private selves run underneath. A master's touch keeps the confection thoughtful to the end.
tales-of-the-wilderness:
Boris Andreyevich Vogau, who wrote as Boris Pilniak, is the author of Tales of the Wilderness, rendered into English by F. O'Dempsey. Prince D. S. Mirsky adds a long opening essay, and eleven tales are listed, among them The Snow, A Year of Their Lives, Over the Ravine, and The Heirs.

Mirsky argues that English readers know the great age of Russian prose from Turgenev to Chekhov, yet know little of what came next. He faults the fame given to lesser names while stronger new voices stay unread. Readers get both a plea for fresh Russian writing and Pilniak's own tales of snow, land, and hard lives.
the-atheist-s-mass:
Honoré de Balzac's tale, turned into English by Clara Bell and dedicated to Auguste Borget, centers on two doctors. Bianchon, the narrator's friend, owed science a fine system of the theory of the body and won early fame in the medical school of Paris. He practiced surgery long before he took up medicine.

His first studies were guided by Desplein, one of the greatest of French surgeons, who flashed across science like a meteor. Even his foes granted that Desplein took an unteachable method to the tomb with him. Balzac likens a surgeon's glory to an actor's: both live only while they live, and their talent leaves no trace behind. Against that fading fame the mass of the title will be set.
the-ball-and-the-cross:
G. K. Chesterton's novel opens in a flying ship built by Professor Lucifer, singing through the sky like a silver arrow. Two men ride in a craft filled with tools grown strange and mad. A thing like a huge key with wheels turns out to be a deadly revolver.

Chapter headings promise debate from the start: a discussion in the air, a magistrate's religion, a peacemaker, and another philosopher. Later come a village scandal, a desert island, a garden of peace, and dreams for MacIan and Turnbull. Swords are rejoined, faces pose a riddle, and a last parley leads toward a closing Dies Irae.
the-blue-book-of-chess: The Blue Book of Chess is a guide that claims to teach the first steps of the game and to study all the known openings. It is a new form of a work based on Staunton and on later chess writers, put out in Philadelphia by the John C. Winston Company. Real games show the play, with names such as Morphy, Staunton, Lasker, Steinitz, and Pillsbury on the title page. A note adds that eighty-five of those games are also given in Portable Game Notation.
the-complete-poetical-works-of-edgar-all:
John H. Ingram edited this collection of Edgar Allan Poe's poetical works, and his preface argues its claim at length. Earlier collections, he says, were verbatim reprints of the first posthumous gathering, published at New York in 1850. That held true for American and English editions alike until his own work began.

In 1874 Ingram began calling attention to unknown and unreprinted poetry by Poe still in existence. Most of those specimens later appeared in other editors' pages, but this volume first gathers all of them into one sheaf. It also adds pieces and extra stanzas nowhere else published, drawn from printed and manuscript sources over many years of research. The notes, he adds, carry much matter of their own. Readers thus get an edition built as a recovery project, restoring poems and stanzas that the standard reprints had left scattered or lost.
the-cost-of-kindness:
Jerome K. Jerome opens The Cost of Kindness at the Pennycoops' table, where little Mrs. Pennycoop argues that kindness costs nothing. Her husband George, an auctioneer of twenty years' standing, answers that kindness is generally valued at just what it costs. The two are debating a farewell call on a departing neighbor.

The man in question is old Cracklethorpe, their vicar, whom George calls a disagreeable, cantankerous old brute. In three years, George says, the vicar has made every member of his flock hate the very sight of a church. Mrs. Pennycoop urges patience, holding that trials are sent for our good, while George notes that she, not being churchwarden, can escape the man more easily than he can.
the-country-beyond-a-romance-of-the-wild:
James Oliver Curwood calls The Country Beyond a romance of the wilderness. Curwood wrote The Valley of Silent Men and The Flaming Forest. He sets the tale near the rugged north shore of Lake Superior, south of the Kaministiqua and north of the Rainy River waterway.

Chapter I calls that country a paradise lost in a wilderness world, with a little corner of hell inside it. A girl once named it so, sobbing out her shame and pain before Peter came into her life and leavened its drab weight. From the bald top of Cragg's Ridge on a fine thirtieth of May, no one would guess at that hell. Picture captions name the pair Peter and Nada and carry her whisper: We'll make it, Peter.
the-daughter-of-an-empress: Louise Muhlbach's The Daughter of an Empress is shown here only through its long contents list. The headings name Countess Natalie Dolgorucki, Count Munnich, Count Ostermann, a night of conspiracy, the Regent Anna Leopoldowna, Princess Elizabeth, and a revolution. Diplomatic quarrels, Pope Ganganelli (Clement XIV), a festival of Cardinal Bernis, Alexis Orloff, and an invasion follow. Only the title page and that list are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
the-errand-boy-or-how-phil-brent-won-suc:
Horatio Alger Jr.'s The Errand Boy; or, How Phil Brent Won Success opens with a snowball. Phil Brent, trudging home through snow to his stepmother's house, takes a hard, wet ball below the ear and spins round, eyes flashing, to find who threw it. No one shows but a mild old man in spectacles, picking through the drifts.

Phil's stepbrother is the true culprit, as the tale soon shows. Fired, cheated, and cast off, Phil rises by grit and honesty in New York. Two short tales, Fred Sargent's Revenge and The Smuggler's Trap, fill out the book.
the-free-press:
Hilaire Belloc wrote The Free Press as a short essay on why small, free papers beat the great press, first printed in 1918. A letter at the front gives the book to Orage, editor of The New Age.

Belloc recalls days when The New Age was the one paper where truth about crooked politics could be told. He pairs it with the New Witness, though the two hold opposed faiths. Both lack big ads and wide sales, yet sway events out of all scale to their size. Belloc argues that owned papers serve wealth and power, while poor, free ones can say what they see.
the-free-rangers-a-story-of-the-early-da:
Joseph A. Altsheler wrote The Free Rangers as a tale of early days along the Mississippi, first printed in 1909. It goes on with the boys of his Young Trailers tales.

A note at the front says the story stands alone. Yet it keeps up the fortunes of two boys and their friends. Those friends come from The Young Trailers and The Forest Runners. They come from The Eyes of the Woods too. Altsheler's young scouts range a wild river land. French, Spanish, and native foes fill that land. Skill in the woods, bold marches, and fights for new settlements fill his tales. He wrote to give boys a heroic past on the frontier.
the-freebooters-of-the-wilderness:
Agnes C. Laut wrote The Freebooters of the Wilderness as a novel of the west, printed at New York in 1913. Two parts divide the tale, the first ending with a desert and bitter waters.

The contents name hard choices from the start: to straddle or fight, cards stacked, law marking time while crime scores. A handy man gets busy, tracks all point one way, and the majesty of the law veils itself. Laut, author of The Conquest of the Great Northwest, writes of land fraud and range greed, where men who steal whole valleys hide behind slow courts and bought help.
the-history-of-a-crime-the-testimony-of-: Victor Hugo wrote The History of a Crime. The subtitle calls it the testimony of an eye-witness. T. H. Joyce and Arthur Locker translated the book. The contents divide the account into days. The First Day is headed The Ambush. Its chapters include Paris Sleeps — the Bell Rings. Later chapters include Violation of the Chamber and Mazas. The Second Day is headed The Struggle. What is present here stops with the front matter. The account itself does not appear.
the-hour-glass:
W. B. Yeats wrote The Hour-Glass, subtitled a morality. The cast lists a Wise Man, a Fool, some pupils, an Angel, and the Wise Man's wife and two children. The scene is a large room with a desk and chair in the middle, benches, and an hour-glass on a bracket near the door.

The Wise Man turns the pages of a book, seeking a passage to explain to his pupils that day. The passage, said to come from a beggar who wrote on Babylon's walls, speaks of two living countries, one visible and one invisible. He finds the words hard and close to foolishness. A Fool enters with shears in hand, holds out his hat, and asks for a penny.
the-iceberg-express:
David Cory wrote the linked fairy tales in this children's book. The contents promise a magic comb and a coral palace. King Seaphus, an enchanted prince, and magic seeds follow. Candy City and Toy Land close the list. The first tale opens on a bright August morning. Little Mary Louise is trusted out alone for the first time. Her family has moved to the seashore for the summer. She crosses the meadow to the beach. The tide crowds in like children hurrying home from school.

She wonders who urges the waves onward. A hoarse, hollow voice seems to push them. What lies beneath and beyond the sea? White ships glide there, smaller than seabirds. A low rippling laugh reaches her ear. An older girl rests on the sand nearby. The girl is tired from swimming. Cory builds his undersea adventures from a small girl's questions. A strange companion answers them.
the-life-and-letters-of-elizabeth-prenti:
George L. Prentiss prepared the memoir of his wife Elizabeth, author of Stepping Heavenward, at the request of her old friends. His opening summary says much of the book works as autobiography. Her letters and journal extracts form the larger share, starting in her twentieth year and running almost to her death.

A sketch of her father Edward Payson and notes on others who shaped her fill out the story. The dated preface closes at Kauinfels in September 1882. Christian readers were the hoped audience, since Elizabeth wished her costly experience to strengthen and comfort other souls.
the-life-of-reason-the-phases-of-human-p: George Santayana wrote his philosophy of the life of reason in five volumes, opening with Reason in Common Sense. Only the series title pages and a detailed outline of the first volume subject are present here, summarizing his method and his debts to Greek thinkers. Heraclitus, Democritus, Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle each earn a line in that outline. Santayana argument that progress answers an ideal made by reflection does not unfold in this record beyond the summary.
the-light-princess:
George MacDonald tells his fairy tale of a king and queen with no children. Chapter heads promise a princess who laughs too much, trials of metaphysics and water, and a prince who must be found. The king opens the tale in a sulk over his empty nursery.

He counts queens with three, seven, or twelve children and feels ill used by his own queen patience. MacDonald jokes gently with both parents before a daughter at last arrives. A christening curse will lift her gravity away, leaving a girl too light in body and mind until love and tears teach weight.
the-little-duke-richard-the-fearless:
Charlotte M. Yonge wrote The Little Duke: Richard the Fearless, first published in 1854. This copy is the 1905 Macmillan edition, whose title page credits only the author of The Heir of Redclyffe. Chapter one opens in the Castle of Bayeux in Normandy on an autumn day in the year 943. Servants prepare a great hall for Duke William's supper while Dame Astrida directs the work and watches for the hunting party. Young Richard bursts in flourishing his bow, proud that he hit a stag in the neck.

Yonge gives young readers a boy duke growing up amid feasts, hunts, and danger in early Normandy. The hall, with its rushes, silver cups, and smoke-filled roof, is described in rich detail before the story moves on.
the-man-of-letters-as-a-man-of-business:
William Dean Howells's essay "The Man of Letters as a Man of Business" begins from a hard doctrine. Every man ought to work for his living, and no man ought to live by an art. Art should be a privilege exercised after daily bread is earned, and its results free to all. People feel instinctively, Howells says, that there is something profane in taking money for a picture, a poem, or a statue, and the artist feels it most of all. He grants the defenses: priests, physicians, and justice itself are paid, and an artist who does not sell will starve.

All the same, the sin and shame remain. In a second section he calls literature the most intimate and articulate of the arts, the mind speaking to the mind, which exists only when put into terms of invariable significance. Business, his opening declares, is the opprobrium of literature.
the-nature-of-goodness:
George Herbert Palmer's The Nature of Goodness, dated 1903, grew out of lectures by Harvard's Alford Professor of Philosophy. A preface lists the audiences who heard its substance: Harvard, Dartmouth, Wellesley, Western Reserve, the University of California, and Boston's Twentieth Century Club. Parts of the sixth chapter served as addresses to Harvard's Phi Beta Kappa Society and Berkeley's Philosophical Union.

Searching criticism from those audiences, Palmer writes, helped clear his thought and simplify its expression. His earlier Field of Ethics had marked out the place ethics occupies among the sciences. This book examines the first problem of ethics itself, and the two volumes together were meant as an easy yet serious introduction. Chapter I is titled The Double Aspect of Goodness.
the-people-of-the-abyss: Jack London's 1903 exposé of the East End slums, where he lived for weeks disguised as an out-of-work sailor. Starvation wages, doss-houses, and broken lives are documented with furious compassion. The book that forced comfortable England to look at its poor, and a landmark of undercover journalism.
the-princess:
Alfred Lord Tennyson's poem The Princess begins with a prologue set on Sir Walter Vivian's lawns. On a summer's day Sir Walter has given his broad lawns to the people until sunset. Tenants flock there at noon, and half the neighbouring borough with its Institute, of which he is patron. The narrator is home from college, visiting Walter's son with five others of their set. They are seven at Vivian-place.

That morning Walter shows the house, Greek in style and set with busts. Carved stones from the abbey ruin in the park lie on the pavement. Tables hold a jumble of every clime and age: celts, calumets, claymores, and snowshoes. Ancestral arms hang between the horns of elk and deer. Walter brings out a family chronicle of knights, half legend and half history. One lady in it armed her own head and beat her foes from her walls.
the-prospector-a-tale-of-the-crow-s-nest:
Ralph Connor's The Prospector opens on a rare November day of purple haze and slanting yellow light. Chapter I, A Social Impossibility, sets the scene before the contents' promised trail: varsity against McGill, a voice in the wilderness, and only one claim. Later chapters name the outpost, the old prospector, Tim Carroll, and a turf meet. The motto 'I was a stranger, and ye took me in' heads one chapter.

Nature wears a face of content, having fulfilled her course and settling toward winter sleep. The grass stays vividly green and the trees stand softened in the haze. A good day to be alive, the narrator calls it, the air's tingle getting into the blood. The contents close with the waiting game and the region beyond.
the-rome-express:
Arthur Griffiths wrote The Rome Express, issued in 1907 with a frontispiece in colours by Arthur O. Scott. The contents list twenty chapters, none of them titled, so the shape of the mystery is left to the reading.

Chapter one places the Rome Express, called the direttissimo, on its final hundred-mile run from Laroche into Paris one March morning. Word spreads through the sleeping-car that something is very much amiss there. Seven people had occupied the car, six were seen at the early breakfast halt, and the account breaks off as the discrepancy begins to emerge.
the-slim-princess: George Ade's The Slim Princess was published in 1907. A note explains its origin at length. The book was elaborated and rewritten from a story in The Saturday Evening Post late in 1906. The pages shown give that note and a contents list only. Woman in Morovenia opens the thirteen chapters. Kalora's affliction and the cruelty of law follow. He arrives and he departs come next. The governor cables near the end, before the home-coming.
the-southern-cross: Foxhall Daingerfield Jr. wrote this play in four acts, produced at the Opera House in Lexington, Kentucky, on April 13, 1909, for the benefit of the Morgan Monument, and copyrighted that year. The pages present here give the title and dedication to the memory of General John Hunt Morgan. A cast list follows, naming Gordon Cabell, played by Mr. McComas, so the dialogue itself does not appear.
the-story-of-the-pony-express:
Glenn D. Bradley, author of Winning the Southwest, states one purpose in his preface. He aims at a true, useful, and readable account. Its subject is the most remarkable mail service ever known. The Pony Express played an important part in history, he argues. It showed what American spirit can accomplish. The heroes of sixty-one, he says, were not all southerners fighting each other.

Bradley brings to light the enterprise's inception, organization, and development, its historical background, and anecdotes of its operation, while trying not to drown the central topic in fascinating western adventure. He acknowledges Frank A. Root's joint work on the overland stage to California, Senate documents, Inman and Cody's Salt Lake Trail, old newspaper files, Bancroft's history of the West, and writings of Samuel L. Clemens.
the-theology-of-holiness: Dougan Clark, professor of systematic theology at Earlham College, wrote The Theology of Holiness and dedicated it to his parents, both approved ministers in the Friends' Church. The pages present here give his portrait, the title, the dedication, and a contents list that runs to sixteen chapters. Those chapters argue entire sanctification as a necessity, trace it through patriarchs, types, and prophecy, and follow its teaching in Jesus, Paul, Peter, John, James, and Jude. Chapter one is named but not begun, so Clark's argument stands outlined only.
the-voyage-of-the-hoppergrass:
Edmund Lester Pearson addresses The Voyage of the Hoppergrass to his nephew Philip in a letter dated July 28, 1913, the anniversary of the Hoppergrass sailing. The story, he says, concerns boys and men, with two kinds of pirates. One kind suits readers from about eight to sixteen, and the other from sixteen up to ninety-seven or ninety-eight.

Pearson cheerfully lends the book onward to fathers and sisters once Philip finishes it. Contents pages list seven chapters, from the beginning of the voyage through a man on a desert island and the last of the pirates. Well buried treasure, midnight burglars, and offered lodgings follow before the party decides to go.
the-witness:
Grace Livingston Hill Lutz wrote The Witness, a novel copyrighted in 1917 by Harper and Brothers. Lutz dedicates the book to her mother, Marcia MacDonald Livingston. A verse from First John gives the title its meaning. The first chapter opens in a college dormitory after dinner. Quiet study hours suddenly give way to uproar.

Doors slam and heavy bodies rush down the corridor. Voices echo and even the electric lights seem to tremble. Lutz builds a lively campus scene in a few strokes. The contrast between peace and chaos sets the story moving. Readers can expect a tale where faith is tested amid everyday pressures.
theodore-roosevelt-and-his-times-a-chron:
Harold Howland subtitled his book a chronicle of the Progressive movement, and its sixteen chapters follow Roosevelt from young fighter to his last four years. Assembly fights, civil service reform, and battles with boss Platt come before the presidency. Square Deal chapters treat business, labour, reclamation, and conservation.

Chapter one borrows Browning's line, I was ever a fighter, as Roosevelt's epitaph. Howland recalls a sickly, asthmatic boy whose father built him a gymnasium on East Twentieth Street. Readers get a political life framed as one long contest, beginning with the fight for health.
thoughts-suggested-by-mr-froude-s-progre:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote an essay prompted by Mr. Froude's Progress, starting from the common wish to revisit earth centuries later. Merely watching from a distant sphere would not satisfy most people, he says. They would want to feel the future world's passions and hopes.

Warner mocks critics who sit on the fence, calling life a cheap performance with tattered flags and dusty soldiers. Underneath, he finds a near universal belief that the world will progress and grow more interesting. Readers get a reflective American essay asking whether the golden age lies behind or ahead, never in the poor present.
through-the-brazilian-wilderness:
Theodore Roosevelt begins his Brazilian travel book by recalling a 1908 call from Father Zahm, a priest friend fond of Dante, history, and science. Zahm proposed crossing the Andes and descending the Amazon together after Roosevelt's presidency ended. Roosevelt then preferred Africa, and the idea slept for five years.

In 1913 lecture invitations from Argentina and Brazil revived it. Roosevelt chose to return north through the continent's middle and the Amazon valley. He consulted the American Museum of Natural History about taking naturalists to collect specimens. Readers get a former president planning a scientific expedition into little-known wilderness.
through-the-looking-glass: Lewis Carroll arranged Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There, as a chess game before the story begins. A cast list assigns pieces and pawns to Tweedledum and Tweedledee, the Walrus and Carpenter, both queens, Humpty Dumpty, and others. Alice is the white pawn. A chessboard diagram and eleven-move problem follow, mapping Alice's meetings with each queen and her coronation. The cast, board, and move list are what is given in this record, so Carroll's chapters themselves do not appear.
uncle-william-the-man-who-was-shif-less:
Jennette Lee's Uncle William, the man who was shiftless, opens with a poem of dedication to Gerald Stanley Lee. The verses ask for a singer who hears the sunrise coming through the night. Chapter one then gives the singer himself: William Benslow, hitching his trousers up by their one suspender.

Yes, I'm shiftless, William says with satisfaction. He watches a painter friend struggle with a mysterious green in the harbor water. Painting is steady work, too steady for him: sailing suits him better, with lively steps between long sits while the boat skims along by herself. Lee builds a philosophy of contentment out of an old sailor's idle talk.
way-of-the-lawless:
Max Brand published Way of the Lawless in 1921, noting that it first appeared under the title Free Range. Chapter one stands in a blacksmith shop. Old Jasper Lanning folds his withered arms and studies the young fellow swinging the sledge at the forge. Andrew Lanning is Jasper's life work. With an artist's aching heart, the old man judges that work a failure.

Andy is not even his son. Fifteen years before, the boy's father died. Jasper came riding out of the mountain desert, sudden as a hawk dropping from a pale sky. The boy had black hair and eyes and a well-made jaw. His mouth was too soft for Jasper's taste, since tenderness in men earned none of his sympathy. His own life was littered with hard deeds. Brand sets an outlaw's raising against a boy's softness, and lets the forge fire light both.
why-go-to-college-an-address:
Alice Freeman Palmer, once president of Wellesley College, gave the address Why Go to College? More girls each year, she notes, find college doors open to them. A lawyer friend told her he feared dying and leaving his daughters only a bank account. Mothers, too, have learned that wealth and a fine marriage do not ensure a happy life.

Palmer answers parents who see no need for college if a daughter need not teach. College, she argues, gives stimulus, discipline, knowledge, and wide interests. It readies a girl for the most useful life she can live. Training also guards her if she must earn her own way. Palmer's case is warm, plain, and firm.
